lessons.title: Key Concept - Coulomb's Law
lessons.notes_html:
This book covers Chapters 12 to 21 of the Class 12 Physics book - every question, MCQ and problem, with the book's printed answers.

State Coulomb's law and write its mathematical form.

Coulomb's law states that the force between two point charges is directly proportional to the product of their magnitudes and inversely proportional to the square of the distance between them.

Mathematically, F is proportional to q1 q2 / r squared.

In free space, F = (1 / 4 pi epsilon-zero) x (q1 q2 / r squared).

The constant 1 / 4 pi epsilon-zero equals 9 x 10^9 N m^2 C^-2.

mcqs.q: According to Coulomb's law, the force between two point charges is directly proportional to:
options: The sum of the magnitudes of the two charges
The product of the magnitudes of the two charges
The square of the distance between the charges
The difference of the magnitudes of the two charges
mcqs.why: Coulomb's law states that the force is directly proportional to the product of the magnitudes of the charges and inversely proportional to the square of the distance between them.

mcqs.q: If the distance between two point charges is doubled, the force between them becomes:
options: One half of its original value
One quarter of its original value
mcqs.why: The force varies as 1 / r^2. Replacing r by 2r gives 1 / (2r)^2 = 1 / (4 r^2), so the force falls to 1 / 4 = 0.25 of its original value.

mcqs.q: The mathematical form of Coulomb's law in free space is:
options: F = (1 / 4 pi epsilon-zero) x q1 q2 / r^2
F = (1 / 4 pi epsilon-zero) x q1 q2 / r
F = 4 pi epsilon-zero x q1 q2 / r^2
mcqs.why: In free space the notes give F = (1 / 4 pi epsilon-zero) x (q1 q2 / r^2): the charges multiply, the distance is squared, and the constant 1 / (4 pi epsilon-zero) multiplies the whole expression.

mcqs.q: The value of the constant 1 / (4 pi epsilon-zero) is:
mcqs.why: The notes state that the constant 1 / (4 pi epsilon-zero) equals 9 x 10^9 N m^2 C^-2, the value used in every Coulomb's law calculation in this chapter.

mcqs.q: Both charges are doubled while their separation stays the same. The force between them becomes:
options: The same as the original force
mcqs.why: The force is proportional to q1 q2. Doubling each charge multiplies the product by 2 x 2 = 4, so the force becomes four times the original force.

mcqs.q: One charge is tripled and the distance between the charges is also tripled. The new force is:
options: One ninth of the original force
One third of the original force
mcqs.why: The numerator q1 q2 grows by a factor of 3 while the denominator r^2 grows by 3^2 = 9. The force changes by 3 / 9 = 1 / 3, so the new force is one third of the original.

mcqs.q: Two point charges of 2 microC and 3 microC are placed 0.10 m apart in free space. The force between them is:
The SI unit of the constant 1 / (4 pi epsilon-zero) is:
mcqs.why: The notes give the constant as 9 x 10^9 N m^2 C^-2: newtons times metre squared per coulomb squared, exactly the unit needed for F = (1 / 4 pi epsilon-zero) q1 q2 / r^2 to give a force in newtons.

mcqs.q: Two equal charges repel each other with force F. If their separation is halved, the force becomes:
mcqs.why: The force varies as 1 / r^2. Halving the distance gives 1 / (r / 2)^2 = 4 / r^2, which is 4 times the original 1 / r^2, so the force becomes 4 F.

mcqs.q: In the expression F = (1 / 4 pi epsilon-zero) x q1 q2 / r^2, if r is increased, the force:
options: Decreases, because r^2 is in the denominator
Increases, because r^2 is in the denominator
Stays the same, because r cancels out
Decreases, because q1 q2 is in the numerator
mcqs.why: The distance appears as r^2 in the denominator of Coulomb's law, so a larger separation means a smaller force: the force is inversely proportional to the square of the distance.

lessons.title: Review Questions
lessons.notes_html:
12.1. The potential is constant throughout a given region of space. Is the electrical field zero or non-zero in this region? Explain.

The electric field is zero in this region.

The field is the negative rate of change of potential with distance, E = - (change in V) / (change in r).

If V is constant, its change is zero, so E = 0.

There is no field where the potential does not vary from point to point.

12.2. Suppose that you follow an electric field line due to a positive point charge. Do electric field and the potential increase or decrease?

Both decrease as you move away from the positive charge.

The field of a point charge is E = kQ / r squared, which falls as r grows.

The potential is V = kQ / r, which also falls as r grows.

Field lines point from higher potential to lower potential, so moving along a field line means moving to lower potential.

12.3. How can you identify that which plate of a capacitor is positively charged?

The positively charged plate is the one at the higher potential.

Electric field lines start on the positive plate and end on the negative plate.

A small positive test charge placed between the plates is pushed away from the positive plate and pulled towards the negative plate.

In a circuit, it is the plate joined to the positive terminal of the battery.

12.4. Describe the force or forces on a positive point charge when placed between parallel plates (a) with similar and equal charges (b) with opposite and equal charges.

(a) Similar and equal charges: the field of one plate cancels the field of the other between the plates.

The net field between the plates is zero, so no force acts on the charge there.

(b) Opposite and equal charges: the fields of the two plates add between the plates.

The result is a uniform field pointing from the positive plate to the negative plate.

The charge feels a force F = qE towards the negative plate.

12.5. Electric lines of force never cross. Why?

An electric line of force shows the direction of the field at every point on it.

The field at any one point has a single, unique direction.

If two lines crossed, the field at the crossing point would have two directions at once.

That is impossible, so lines of force never cross.

12.6. If a point charge q of mass m is released in a non-uniform electric field with field lines pointing in the same direction, will it make a rectilinear motion?

Yes, its motion is rectilinear, that is, along a straight line.

The force on the charge is always along the field line, F = qE, and the lines all point the same way.

So the charge keeps moving along that straight direction.

Because the field is non-uniform, the size of the force, and hence the acceleration, changes along the path, but the direction does not.

12.7. Is E necessarily zero inside a charged rubber balloon if balloon is spherical?

Assume that charge is distributed uniformly over the surface.

Yes, the field inside is zero everywhere.

Charge on a conductor, such as the charged rubber surface, stays on the outer surface.

By symmetry, and by Gauss's law for a spherical shell, the fields of all the surface charges cancel at any inside point.

So E = 0 inside the uniformly charged spherical balloon.

12.8. Is it true that Gauss's law states that the total number of lines of force crossing any closed surface in the outward direction is proportional to the net positive charge enclosed within surface?

Yes, this statement is true.

Gauss's law says the total electric flux through a closed surface equals the enclosed charge divided by epsilon-zero.

The number of lines of force crossing the surface is a picture of that flux.

So the outward lines are proportional to the net positive charge enclosed.

12.9. Do electrons tend to go to region of high potential or of low potential?

Electrons tend to go to the region of high potential.

The field points from high potential to low potential.

The force on a negative charge is opposite to the field, F = -eE.

So an electron is pushed towards higher potential, against the field direction.

lessons.title: Numerical Problems - Worked in Full
lessons.notes_html:
12.1. Compare magnitudes of electrical and gravitational forces exerted on an object (mass = 10.0 g, charge = 20.0 microC) by an identical object placed 10.0 cm from the first. (G = 6.67 x 10^-11 N m^2 kg^-2) (Book answer: Fe/Fg = 5.4 x 10^14)

Convert to SI units: m = 10.0 g = 0.010 kg, q = 20.0 microC = 20.0 x 10^-6 C, r = 10.0 cm = 0.10 m.

Electrical force: Fe = k q squared / r squared.

Fe = (9.0 x 10^9) x (20.0 x 10^-6) squared / (0.10) squared.

(20.0 x 10^-6) squared = 400 x 10^-12 = 4.0 x 10^-10.

Fe = (9.0 x 10^9) x (4.0 x 10^-10) / 0.010 = 3.6 / 0.010 = 360 N.

Gravitational force: Fg = G m squared / r squared.

Fg = (6.67 x 10^-11) x (0.010) squared / (0.10) squared.

Fg = (6.67 x 10^-11) x (1.0 x 10^-4) / 0.010 = 6.67 x 10^-13 N.

Ratio: Fe / Fg = 360 / (6.67 x 10^-13) = 5.4 x 10^14.

Answer: Fe / Fg = 5.4 x 10^14, as printed in the book.

12.2. Calculate vectorially the net electrostatic force on q as shown in the figure. Charges: q = 4.0 microC at the top, q1 = 1.0 microC and q2 = -1.0 microC at the base corners; each slant side 1.0 m, base halves 0.60 m, height 0.80 m. (Book answer: F = 0.058 i-hat N - see note)

Step 1: Force on q due to q1. Both are positive, so it is repulsion, away from q1, along the left slant.

Magnitude: F1 = k q q1 / r squared = (9.0 x 10^9)(4.0 x 10^-6)(1.0 x 10^-6) / (1.0) squared.

F1 = 0.036 N.

Step 2: Resolve F1. From q1 to q the displacement is (0.60 m across, 0.80 m up) over 1.0 m, so the unit vector is (0.60, 0.80).

F1 vector = 0.036 x (0.60 i-hat + 0.80 j-hat) = 0.0216 i-hat + 0.0288 j-hat N.

Step 3: Force on q due to q2. q2 is negative, so it is attraction, towards q2, along the right slant.

Magnitude: F2 = k q |q2| / r squared = 0.036 N, the same as F1.

Step 4: Resolve F2. From q to q2 the displacement is (0.60 m across, 0.80 m down) over 1.0 m, so the unit vector is (0.60, -0.80).

F2 vector = 0.036 x (0.60 i-hat - 0.80 j-hat) = 0.0216 i-hat - 0.0288 j-hat N.

Step 5: Add the vectors. The j-hat parts cancel: 0.0288 - 0.0288 = 0.

The i-hat parts add: 0.0216 + 0.0216 = 0.0432.

Component-wise result: F = 0.043 i-hat N.

NOTE ON THE PRINTED ANSWER: the book prints F = 0.058 i-hat N, which is 2 x 0.036 x 0.80 = 0.0576 N, that is, it uses 0.80 where the figure's x-component ratio is 0.60 / 1.0 = 0.60. The step-by-step addition from the figure's own numbers gives 0.043 i-hat N; the book's printed 0.058 i-hat N is recorded here as printed, not silently substituted.

12.3. A point charge q = -8.0 x 10^-8 C is placed at the origin. Calculate electric field at a point 2.0 m from the origin on the z-axis. [Book answer: (-1.8 x 10^2 k-hat) N C^-1] Field of a point charge: E = k q / r squared, in the direction away from a positive charge and towards a negative charge.

Magnitude: |E| = (9.0 x 10^9)(8.0 x 10^-8) / (2.0) squared.

|E| = 720 / 4.0 = 180 = 1.8 x 10^2 N C^-1.

The charge is negative, so at a point on the +z-axis the field points back towards the origin, that is, in the -k-hat direction.

Answer: E = (-1.8 x 10^2 k-hat) N C^-1, as printed in the book.

12.4. Determine the electric field at the position r = (4 i-hat + 3 j-hat) m caused by a point charge q = 5.0 x 10^-6 C placed at origin. [Book answer: (1440 i-hat + 1080 j-hat) N C^-1] Distance from origin: r = sqrt(4 squared + 3 squared) = sqrt(25) = 5.0 m.

Unit vector along r: r-hat = (4 i-hat + 3 j-hat) / 5 = 0.80 i-hat + 0.60 j-hat.

Field magnitude: E = k q / r squared = (9.0 x 10^9)(5.0 x 10^-6) / (5.0) squared.

E = 45000 / 25 = 1800 N C^-1.

Vector: E = 1800 x (0.80 i-hat + 0.60 j-hat).

E = 1440 i-hat + 1080 j-hat N C^-1.

Answer: (1440 i-hat + 1080 j-hat) N C^-1, as printed in the book.

12.5. Two point charges, q1 = -1.0 x 10^-6 C and q2 = +4.0 x 10^-6 C, are separated by a distance of 3.0 m. Find and justify the zero-field location. (Book answer: 3.0 m)

The zero-field point cannot lie between the charges, because there the two fields point the same way and add.

It cannot lie beyond the larger charge q2, because q2 always dominates there.

It must lie beyond the smaller charge q1, on the side away from q2.

Let its distance from q1 be x. Its distance from q2 is then x + 3.0 m.

Set the magnitudes equal: k |q1| / x squared = k |q2| / (x + 3.0) squared.

Cancel k and take square roots: (x + 3.0) / x = sqrt(|q2| / |q1|) = sqrt(4.0) = 2.

So x + 3.0 = 2x, giving x = 3.0 m.

Answer: 3.0 m from q1, on the side away from q2, as printed in the book.

12.6. Find the electric field strength required to hold suspended a particle of mass 1.0 x 10^-6 kg and charge 1.0 microC between two plates 10.0 cm apart.

(Book answer: 9.8 V m^-1) For suspension, the upward electric force must balance the weight: qE = mg.

So E = mg / q.

E = (1.0 x 10^-6 kg)(9.8 m s^-2) / (1.0 x 10^-6 C).

E = 9.8 x 10^-6 / 1.0 x 10^-6 = 9.8 V m^-1.

Answer: 9.8 V m^-1, as printed in the book. (The 10.0 cm plate separation is not needed for E itself; it would give the plate voltage V = E d = 0.98 V.)

12.7. A particle having a charge of 20 electrons on it falls through a potential difference of 100 volts. Calculate the energy acquired by it in electron volts (eV). [Book answer: (2.0 x 10^3 eV)] Charge on the particle: q = 20 e.

Energy gained falling through potential V: Energy = qV.

Energy = 20 e x 100 V = 2000 eV.

Answer: 2.0 x 10^3 eV, as printed in the book.

12.8. Millikan's experiment: oil droplets between two flat horizontal plates, 5.00 mm apart. Plate voltage adjusted to exactly 780 V so the droplet is held stationary. Voltage switched off; the droplet falls 1.50 mm in 11.2 s. Density of oil 900 kg m^-3, viscosity of air 1.80 x 10^-5 N s m^-2. Calculate (a) the mass, (b) the charge on the droplet (g = 9.8 m s^-2). [Book answers: (a) 5.14 x 10^-15 kg, (b) 3.20 x 10^-19 C]

Step 1: Terminal velocity of fall: v = distance / time = 1.50 x 10^-3 m / 11.2 s = 1.34 x 10^-4 m s^-1.

Step 2: At terminal velocity the Stokes drag balances the weight: 6 pi eta r v = mg, with m = (4/3) pi r cubed x density.

Step 3: Solve for the radius: r squared = 9 eta v / (2 x density x g). r squared = 9 x (1.80 x 10^-5) x (1.34 x 10^-4) / (2 x 900 x 9.8). r squared = 2.17 x 10^-8 / 17640 = 1.23 x 10^-12, so r = 1.11 x 10^-6 m.

Step 4: Mass: m = (4/3) pi r cubed x density = (4/3) pi (1.11 x 10^-6) cubed x 900. m = 5.14 x 10^-15 kg. Answer (a) matches the book.

Step 5: When held stationary, electric force balances weight: qE = mg, with E = V / d.

E = 780 V / 5.00 x 10^-3 m = 1.56 x 10^5 V m^-1.

Step 6: q = mg / E = (5.14 x 10^-15)(9.8) / (1.56 x 10^5). q = 5.04 x 10^-14 / 1.56 x 10^5 = 3.20 x 10^-19 C. Answer (b) matches the book.

The charge is twice the elementary charge 1.60 x 10^-19 C, as expected for a quantized charge.

12.9. A proton placed in a uniform electric field of 5000 N C^-1 directed to right is allowed to go a distance of 10.0 cm from A to B. Calculate (a) potential difference between the two points (b) work done by the field (c) change in P.E. of proton (d) change in K.E. of the proton (e) its velocity (mass of proton 1.67 x 10^-27 kg). (Book answers: -500 V, 500 eV, -500 eV, 500 eV, 3.097 x 10^5 m s^-1)

Step 1: (a) Moving along the field, potential falls: V(B) - V(A) = -E d.

V(B) - V(A) = -(5000)(0.10) = -500 V.

Step 2: (b) Work done by the field: W = q E d = (1.60 x 10^-19 C)(5000 N C^-1)(0.10 m).

W = 8.0 x 10^-17 J. In electron volts: 8.0 x 10^-17 / 1.60 x 10^-19 = 500 eV.

Step 3: (c) Change in potential energy is the negative of the work done by the field.

Change in P.E. = -500 eV.

Step 4: (d) By energy conservation, the lost potential energy becomes kinetic energy.

Change in K.E. = +500 eV.

Step 5: (e) (1/2) m v squared = 8.0 x 10^-17 J. v squared = 2 x (8.0 x 10^-17) / (1.67 x 10^-27) = 9.58 x 10^10. v = 3.097 x 10^5 m s^-1.

Answers: -500 V, 500 eV, -500 eV, 500 eV, 3.097 x 10^5 m s^-1, as printed in the book.

12.10. Using zero reference point at infinity, determine the amount by which a point charge of 4.0 x 10^-8 C alters the electric potential at a point 1.2 m away, when (a) charge is positive (b) charge is negative. (Book answers: +3.0 x 10^2 V, -3.0 x 10^2 V)

Potential of a point charge with zero at infinity: V = k q / r.

(a) Positive charge: V = (9.0 x 10^9)(4.0 x 10^-8) / 1.2.

V = 360 / 1.2 = 300 = +3.0 x 10^2 V.

(b) Negative charge: q = -4.0 x 10^-8 C, so V = -300 V.

Answers: +3.0 x 10^2 V and -3.0 x 10^2 V, as printed in the book.

12.11. In Bohr's atomic model of hydrogen atom, the electron is in an orbit around the nuclear proton at a distance of 5.29 x 10^-11 m with a speed of 2.18 x 10^6 m s^-1 (e = 1.60 x 10^-19 C, mass of electron = 9.10 x 10^-31 kg). Find (a) the electric potential that a proton exerts at this distance (b) total energy of the atom in eV (c) the ionization energy for the atom in eV. (Book answers: +27.20 V, -13.6 eV, +13.60 eV)

Step 1: (a) Potential due to the proton: V = k e / r.

V = (9.0 x 10^9)(1.60 x 10^-19) / (5.29 x 10^-11).

V = 1.44 x 10^-9 / 5.29 x 10^-11 = 27.20 V.

Step 2: (b) Kinetic energy of the electron: K.E. = (1/2) m v squared.

K.E. = 0.5 x (9.10 x 10^-31) x (2.18 x 10^6) squared.

K.E. = 0.5 x (9.10 x 10^-31) x (4.75 x 10^12) = 2.16 x 10^-18 J.

In eV: 2.16 x 10^-18 / 1.60 x 10^-19 = 13.5 eV.

Step 3: Potential energy: P.E. = -eV = -(1.60 x 10^-19 C)(27.20 V) = -27.2 eV.

Step 4: Total energy = K.E. + P.E. = 13.5 eV - 27.2 eV = -13.6 eV (using the book's rounded values, -13.6 eV).

Step 5: (c) Ionization energy is the energy needed to free the electron, the negative of the total energy.

Ionization energy = +13.60 eV.

Answers: +27.20 V, -13.6 eV, +13.60 eV, as printed in the book.

12.12. The electronic flash attachment for a camera contains a capacitor for storing the energy used to produce the flash. In one such unit, the potential difference between the plates of a 750 microF capacitor is 330 V. Determine the energy that is used to produce the flash. (Book answer: 40.8 J)

Energy stored in a capacitor: U = (1/2) C V squared.

C = 750 microF = 750 x 10^-6 F, V = 330 V.

U = 0.5 x (750 x 10^-6) x (330) squared.

(330) squared = 108900.

U = 0.5 x (750 x 10^-6) x 108900 = 0.5 x 81.675 = 40.8 J.

Answer: 40.8 J, as printed in the book.

12.13. A capacitor has a capacitance of 2.5 x 10^-8 F. In the charging process, electrons are removed from one plate and placed on the other one. When the potential difference between the plates is 450 V, how many electrons have been transferred? (e = 1.60 x 10^-19 C) (Book answer: 7.0 x 10^13 electrons)

Charge stored: Q = C V.

Q = (2.5 x 10^-8 F)(450 V) = 1.125 x 10^-5 C.

Number of electrons: n = Q / e. n = (1.125 x 10^-5) / (1.60 x 10^-19) = 7.03 x 10^13.

Answer: 7.0 x 10^13 electrons, as printed in the book.

mcqs.q: Two identical objects (mass 10.0 g, charge 20.0 microC) are placed 10.0 cm apart. The ratio of the electrical force to the gravitational force between them is:
In the same comparison, the electrical force between the two objects is:

Charges q = 4.0 microC, q1 = 1.0 microC and q2 = -1.0 microC sit at the corners of a triangle with slant sides 1.0 m, base halves 0.60 m and height 0.80 m. Working from the figure's own dimensions, the net force on q is:
mcqs.why: Each force has magnitude 0.036 N. The x-components use the ratio 0.60 / 1.0 = 0.60, giving 0.036 x 0.60 = 0.0216 N each; they add to 0.0432 N while the j-hat parts cancel, so F = 0.043 i-hat N. The book prints 0.058 i-hat N, which wrongly uses 0.80 (the y-ratio) for the x-components; the notes record the printed value but the figure's own numbers give 0.043 i-hat N.

mcqs.q: A point charge q = -8.0 x 10^-8 C is at the origin. The electric field at a point 2.0 m away on the z-axis is:
mcqs.why: Magnitude: |E| = 9.0 x 10^9 x 8.0 x 10^-8 / (2.0)^2 = 720 / 4.0 = 180 = 1.8 x 10^2 N C^-1. The charge is negative, so at a point on the +z-axis the field points back towards the origin, in the -k-hat direction: E = (-1.8 x 10^2 k-hat) N C^-1.

mcqs.q: A point charge q = 5.0 x 10^-6 C at the origin produces, at r = (4 i-hat + 3 j-hat) m, an electric field of:
Two point charges q1 = -1.0 x 10^-6 C and q2 = +4.0 x 10^-6 C are 3.0 m apart. The zero-field point lies:
options: Beyond q2, on the side away from q1
Beyond q1, 3.0 m from q1 on the side away from q2
Between the charges, 1.0 m from q1
mcqs.why: Between the charges the fields add, and beyond the larger charge q2 always dominates, so the point lies beyond the smaller charge q1. Setting k |q1| / x^2 = k |q2| / (x + 3.0)^2 gives (x + 3.0) / x = (4.0)^0.5 = 2, so x + 3.0 = 2x and x = 3.0 m from q1.

mcqs.q: The electric field strength required to hold suspended a particle of mass 1.0 x 10^-6 kg and charge 1.0 microC is:
mcqs.why: For suspension the electric force balances the weight: qE = mg, so E = mg / q = (1.0 x 10^-6 x 9.8) / (1.0 x 10^-6) = (9.8 x 10^-6) / (1.0 x 10^-6) = 9.8 V m^-1.

mcqs.q: A particle carrying a charge of 20 electrons falls through a potential difference of 100 V. The energy it acquires is:
mcqs.why: The charge is q = 20 e, and the energy gained falling through a potential V is qV. Energy = 20 x 100 = 2000 eV = 2.0 x 10^3 eV.

mcqs.q: In Millikan's experiment a droplet held stationary by 780 V across plates 5.00 mm apart, which falls 1.50 mm in 11.2 s when the voltage is switched off, carries a charge of:
mcqs.why: The fall gives the droplet's mass m = 5.14 x 10^-15 kg. lessons.title: Review Questions
lessons.notes_html:
13.1. A potential difference is applied across the ends of a copper wire. What is the effect on the drift velocity of free electrons by (i) increasing the potential difference (ii) decreasing the length and the temperature of the wire The drift velocity is v = I / (n A e), and it is proportional to the electric field in the wire, v is proportional to E = V / L.

(i) Increasing the potential difference: the field E = V / L increases.

The electrons are driven harder, so the drift velocity increases.

(ii) Decreasing the length: at the same potential difference, E = V / L increases because L is smaller.

So the drift velocity increases.

Decreasing the temperature: the metal ions vibrate less, so the electrons collide less often and move more freely.

The resistance falls and the drift velocity increases.

So in both cases the drift velocity increases.

13.2. Do bends in a wire affect its electrical resistance? Explain.

No, bends in a wire do not appreciably affect its resistance.

The resistance of a wire is R = rho L / A, where L is the length measured along the wire, A is its cross-sectional area, and rho is the resistivity of the material.

Bending the wire changes neither its length along the wire, nor its cross-sectional area, nor its material.

So the resistance stays the same; only the shape of the path changes.

13.3. What are the resistances of the resistors given in the figures A and B? What is the tolerance of each? Explain what is meant by the tolerance? (Fig. Q. 13.3: A: Brown, Green, Red, Gold; B: Yellow, White, Orange, Silver) Colour code: Black 0, Brown 1, Red 2, Orange 3, Yellow 4, Green 5, Blue 6, Violet 7, Grey 8, White 9. The first two bands are digits, the third is the multiplier, the fourth is the tolerance.

Resistor A: Brown (1), Green (5), Red (multiplier 10 squared), Gold (tolerance).

Resistance = 15 x 10 squared = 1500 ohm = 1.5 kilo-ohm, tolerance 5 percent (Gold).

Resistor B: Yellow (4), White (9), Orange (multiplier 10 cubed), Silver (tolerance).

Resistance = 49 x 10 cubed = 49000 ohm = 49 kilo-ohm, tolerance 10 percent (Silver).

Tolerance means the permitted variation of the actual resistance from the marked value.

For example, a 1500 ohm resistor with 5 percent tolerance may actually be anywhere from 1425 ohm to 1575 ohm.

13.4. Why does the resistance of a conductor rise with temperature?

In a metal, current is carried by free electrons moving through a lattice of vibrating ions.

When the temperature rises, the ions vibrate with larger amplitude.

The free electrons then collide more often with the ions and lose more of their drift energy.

More collisions mean more opposition to the flow of charge.

So the resistivity, and hence the resistance, of the conductor rises with temperature.

13.5. What are the difficulties in testing whether the filament of a lighted bulb obeys Ohm's law?

Ohm's law, V = IR with R constant, holds only if the physical state, especially the temperature, stays constant.

A lighted bulb filament does not stay at one temperature: the current itself heats it, and its temperature rises far above room temperature.

As it heats, its resistance rises greatly, so the ratio V / I is not constant.

The filament is therefore non-ohmic in use, and a test at one steady temperature is hard to arrange.

Measuring the cold resistance and the hot resistance separately, and keeping the filament at a fixed temperature while varying V, are the practical difficulties.

13.6. Is the filament resistance lower or higher in a 500 W, 220 V light bulb than in a 100 W, 220 V bulb?

For a bulb, power P = V squared / R, so R = V squared / P.

For the 500 W bulb: R = (220) squared / 500 = 48400 / 500 = 96.8 ohm.

For the 100 W bulb: R = (220) squared / 100 = 48400 / 100 = 484 ohm.

The 500 W bulb draws more current at the same voltage, so it must have the smaller resistance.

Answer: the filament resistance is LOWER in the 500 W bulb (about one-fifth of the 100 W bulb's).

13.7. Describe a circuit which will give a continuously varying potential.

A potential divider (rheostat) circuit gives a continuously varying potential.

Connect a rheostat, a long uniform resistance wire with a sliding contact, across the terminals of a battery.

Take the output between one fixed end of the rheostat and the sliding contact.

As the contact slides along the wire, the length of wire in the output part changes smoothly.

The output potential therefore varies continuously from zero up to the full battery voltage.

13.8. Explain why the terminal potential difference of a battery decreases when the current drawn from it is increased?

The terminal potential difference is V = E - I r, where E is the emf and r is the internal resistance of the battery.

When the battery supplies current, part of its emf is used up in driving the current through its own internal resistance.

This lost voltage is I r, and it grows as the current I grows.

So the larger the current drawn, the larger the internal drop, and the smaller the terminal potential difference V.

13.9. What is Wheatstone bridge? How can it be used to determine an unknown resistance?

A Wheatstone bridge is a network of four resistors arranged in a diamond (two parallel branches, each of two resistors in series), with a battery across one diagonal and a galvanometer across the other diagonal.

The bridge is balanced when the galvanometer shows no deflection, meaning no current flows through it.

At balance, the ratio of the resistances in one branch equals the ratio in the other branch, P / Q = R / S.

If three resistances are known and the fourth is unknown, the unknown is found from this balance condition.

For example, if the unknown is S, then S = R x (Q / P), using the three known resistors.

mcqs.q: A potential difference is applied across a copper wire. If the potential difference is increased, the drift velocity of the free electrons:
mcqs.why: The drift velocity is proportional to the electric field in the wire, E = V / L. Increasing the potential difference increases the field, so the electrons are driven harder and the drift velocity increases.

mcqs.q: The same potential difference is applied across a copper wire whose length is decreased. The drift velocity of the electrons:
options: Increases, because E = V / L increases as L gets smaller
Decreases, because there is less wire to travel through
Stays the same, because V is unchanged
mcqs.why: At the same potential difference, E = V / L increases because L is smaller, and the drift velocity is proportional to E, so the drift velocity increases. (Decreasing the temperature also increases it, because the ions vibrate less and the electrons collide less often.)

mcqs.q: Do bends in a wire affect its electrical resistance?
options: Yes, bending increases the length of the wire
No, bending changes neither the length along the wire, the cross-sectional area, nor the material
No, because resistance does not depend on length
mcqs.why: Resistance is R = rho L / A, where L is the length measured along the wire. Bending changes only the shape of the path: L, A and rho are all unchanged, so the resistance stays the same.

mcqs.q: A resistor has colour bands Brown, Green, Red, Gold. Its resistance and tolerance are:
mcqs.why: Brown = 1 and Green = 5 give the digits 15; Red is the multiplier 10^2, and Gold is the 5 percent tolerance band. Resistance = 15 x 10^2 = 1500 ohm = 1.5 k ohm, tolerance 5 percent.

mcqs.q: A resistor has colour bands Yellow, White, Orange, Silver. Its resistance and tolerance are:
mcqs.why: Yellow = 4 and White = 9 give the digits 49; Orange is the multiplier 10^3, and Silver is the 10 percent tolerance band. Resistance = 49 x 10^3 = 49000 ohm = 49 k ohm, tolerance 10 percent.

mcqs.q: The resistance of a metal conductor rises with temperature because:
options: The number of free electrons decreases
The ions vibrate with larger amplitude, so the free electrons collide with them more often
The wire expands and becomes longer only
The resistivity of every material falls with temperature
mcqs.why: When the temperature rises, the lattice ions vibrate with larger amplitude. The free electrons then collide more often with the ions and lose more of their drift energy, so the resistivity, and hence the resistance, rises with temperature.

mcqs.q: The main difficulty in testing whether the filament of a lighted bulb obeys Ohm's law is that:
options: The filament is too thin to connect to a meter
The current heats the filament, so its temperature and resistance keep changing and V / I is not constant
Ohm's law does not apply to any metal
mcqs.why: Ohm's law, V = IR with R constant, holds only if the physical state, especially the temperature, stays constant. A lighted filament heats up far above room temperature and its resistance rises greatly, so the ratio V / I is not constant and the filament is non-ohmic in use.

mcqs.q: Compare the filament resistances of a 500 W, 220 V bulb and a 100 W, 220 V bulb:
options: The 500 W bulb has the higher resistance, 484 ohm
The 500 W bulb has the lower resistance, 96.8 ohm against 484 ohm
The 500 W bulb has a resistance of 2420 ohm
mcqs.why: For a bulb R = V^2 / P. For the 500 W bulb: R = 220^2 / 500 = 48400 / 500 = 96.8 ohm. For the 100 W bulb: R = 48400 / 100 = 484 ohm. The 500 W bulb draws more current at the same voltage, so its filament resistance is lower.

mcqs.q: The terminal potential difference of a battery decreases when more current is drawn from it because:
options: The emf of the battery falls as it is used
The lost volts I r across the internal resistance grow as the current grows
The external resistance increases with current
Charge leaks out of the terminals
mcqs.why: The terminal potential difference is V = E - I r. Part of the emf is used up driving the current through the battery's own internal resistance; this lost voltage I r grows as I grows, so the terminal potential difference V becomes smaller.

mcqs.q: A Wheatstone bridge is balanced when the galvanometer shows no deflection. The balance condition is:
options: P / R = S / Q with all four equal
mcqs.why: At balance no current flows through the galvanometer, and the ratio of the resistances in one branch equals the ratio in the other branch: P / Q = R / S. If S is unknown, it is found from S = R x (Q / P) using the three known resistors.

lessons.title: Numerical Problems - Worked in Full
lessons.notes_html:
13.1. How many electrons pass through an electric bulb in one minute if the 300 mA current is passing through it? (Book answer: 1.12 x 10^20)

Current: I = 300 mA = 0.30 A. Time: t = 1 minute = 60 s.

Charge passed: Q = I t.

Q = 0.30 x 60 = 18 C.

Number of electrons: n = Q / e, with e = 1.60 x 10^-19 C. n = 18 / (1.60 x 10^-19) = 1.125 x 10^20.

Answer: 1.12 x 10^20 electrons, as printed in the book.

13.2. A charge of 90 C passes through a wire in 1 hour and 15 minutes.

What is the current in the wire? (Book answer: 20 mA) Charge: Q = 90 C.

Time: t = 1 hour 15 minutes = 75 minutes = 75 x 60 = 4500 s.

Current: I = Q / t.

I = 90 / 4500 = 0.020 A.

Answer: 20 mA, as printed in the book.

13.3. Find the equivalent resistance of the circuit (Fig. P. 13.3), total current drawn from the source and the current through each resistor. (Fig: R1 = 6 ohm and R2 = 6 ohm in parallel, in series with R3 = 3 ohm; source 6 V.) (Book answer: 6.0 ohm, 1.0 A, 0.5 A, 0.5 A, 1.0 A)

Step 1: Parallel part. R1 and R2 are in parallel: 1 / Rp = 1 / 6 + 1 / 6 = 2 / 6.

So Rp = 3.0 ohm.

Step 2: Equivalent resistance. Rp is in series with R3: Req = 3.0 + 3.0 = 6.0 ohm.

Step 3: Total current from the source: I = V / Req = 6 / 6.0 = 1.0 A.

Step 4: The total current divides equally between the two equal parallel resistors.

Current through R1 = 0.5 A, current through R2 = 0.5 A.

Step 5: The full total current flows through R3, which is in series with the combination.

Current through R3 = 1.0 A.

Answers: 6.0 ohm, 1.0 A, 0.5 A, 0.5 A, 1.0 A, as printed in the book.

13.4. A rectangular bar of iron is 2.0 cm by 2.0 cm in cross section and 40 cm long. Calculate its resistance if the resistivity of iron is 11 x 10^-8 ohm m. (Book answer: 1.1 x 10^-4 ohm)

Cross-sectional area: A = 2.0 cm x 2.0 cm = 4.0 cm squared = 4.0 x 10^-4 m squared.

Length: L = 40 cm = 0.40 m. Resistivity: rho = 11 x 10^-8 ohm m.

Resistance: R = rho L / A.

R = (11 x 10^-8) x 0.40 / (4.0 x 10^-4).

R = (4.4 x 10^-8) / (4.0 x 10^-4) = 1.1 x 10^-4 ohm.

Answer: 1.1 x 10^-4 ohm, as printed in the book.

13.5. The resistance of an iron wire at 0 degrees C is 1 x 10^4 ohm. What is the resistance at 500 degrees C if the temperature coefficient of resistance of iron is 5.2 x 10^-3 K^-1? (Book answer: 3.6 x 10^4 ohm)

Resistance at temperature t: Rt = R0 (1 + alpha t).

Here R0 = 1 x 10^4 ohm, alpha = 5.2 x 10^-3 K^-1, t = 500 degrees C. alpha t = (5.2 x 10^-3) x 500 = 2.6.

Rt = (1 x 10^4) x (1 + 2.6) = (1 x 10^4) x 3.6.

Answer: 3.6 x 10^4 ohm, as printed in the book.

13.6. Calculate terminal potential difference of each of cells in circuit of Fig. P. 13.6. (Fig: 24 V cell with internal resistance 0.10 ohm, 6.0 V cell with internal resistance 0.90 ohm, in a loop with an 8.0 ohm resistor.) (Book answers: 23.8 V, 7.8 V)

Step 1: The two cells oppose each other in the loop, so the net emf is 24 - 6.0 = 18 V.

Step 2: Total resistance in the loop: 0.10 + 8.0 + 0.90 = 9.0 ohm.

Step 3: Loop current: I = 18 / 9.0 = 2.0 A.

Step 4: The 24 V cell is discharging, so its terminal potential difference is V = E - I r.

V = 24 - (2.0)(0.10) = 24 - 0.20 = 23.8 V.

Step 5: The 6.0 V cell is being charged by the larger cell, so its terminal potential difference is V = E + I r.

V = 6.0 + (2.0)(0.90) = 6.0 + 1.8 = 7.8 V.

Answers: 23.8 V and 7.8 V, as printed in the book.

13.7. Find the current which flows in all the resistances of the circuit of Fig.

P. 13.7. (Fig: 9.0 V cell in the left branch, 18 ohm resistor in the middle branch, 6.0 V cell in series with a 12 ohm resistor in the right branch.) (Book answers: 1.25 A, 0.5 A)

Step 1: The left branch is a 9.0 V cell alone, so the potential difference across the middle branch is 9.0 V.

Step 2: Current through the 18 ohm middle resistor: I = V / R = 9.0 / 18 = 0.5 A.

Step 3: In the right loop the two cells drive current the same way round, so the net emf is 9.0 + 6.0 = 15 V.

Step 4: Current through the 12 ohm resistor: I = 15 / 12 = 1.25 A.

Answers: 1.25 A through the 12 ohm resistor and 0.5 A through the 18 ohm resistor, as printed in the book.

13.8. Find the current and power dissipated in each resistance of the circuit, shown in Fig. P. 13.8. (Fig: left branch 6.0 V cell; top-left 1.0 ohm, middle 2.0 ohm, bottom-left 1.0 ohm; top-right 1.0 ohm, right 2.0 ohm, bottom-right 1.0 ohm; right branch 10 V cell.) (Book answers: 0.8 A, 1.4 A, 2.2 A, 0.64 W, 1.96 W, 3.92 W, 9.68 W)

Step 1: Let I1 be the current in the left loop and I2 the current in the right loop. At the middle junction they add, so the middle 2.0 ohm resistor carries I1 + I2.

Step 2: Left loop (6.0 V cell, two 1.0 ohm resistors, middle 2.0 ohm resistor): 6.0 = I1 (1.0 + 1.0) + 2.0 (I1 + I2).

So 6.0 = 4 I1 + 2 I2. (Equation 1)

Step 3: Right loop (10 V cell, two 1.0 ohm resistors, one 2.0 ohm resistor, middle 2.0 ohm resistor): 10 = I2 (1.0 + 2.0 + 1.0) + 2.0 (I1 + I2).

So 10 = 2 I1 + 6 I2. (Equation 2)

Step 4: Solve. Multiply Equation 2 by 2: 20 = 4 I1 + 12 I2. Subtract Equation 1: 14 = 10 I2, so I2 = 1.4 A.

Step 5: From Equation 1: 4 I1 = 6.0 - 2 (1.4) = 6.0 - 2.8 = 3.2, so I1 = 0.8 A.

Step 6: Middle current: I1 + I2 = 0.8 + 1.4 = 2.2 A.

Step 7: Powers, P = I squared R. Left 1.0 ohm resistors: (0.8) squared x 1.0 = 0.64 W each.

Right 1.0 ohm resistors: (1.4) squared x 1.0 = 1.96 W each.

Right 2.0 ohm resistor: (1.4) squared x 2.0 = 3.92 W.

Middle 2.0 ohm resistor: (2.2) squared x 2.0 = 9.68 W.

Answers: 0.8 A, 1.4 A, 2.2 A, 0.64 W, 1.96 W, 3.92 W, 9.68 W, as printed in the book.

mcqs.why: Charge passed: Q = I t = 0.30 x 60 = 18 C. Number of electrons: n = Q / e = 18 / (1.60 x 10^-19) = 1.125 x 10^20, printed as 1.12 x 10^20.

mcqs.q: A charge of 90 C passes through a wire in 1 hour and 15 minutes. The current in the wire is:
Resistors of 6 ohm and 6 ohm are in parallel, and this combination is in series with a 3 ohm resistor across a 6 V source. The equivalent resistance of the circuit is:
mcqs.why: For the parallel pair, 1 / Rp = 1 / 6 + 1 / 6 = 2 / 6, so Rp = 3.0 ohm. In series with the 3 ohm resistor: Req = 3.0 + 3.0 = 6.0 ohm.

mcqs.q: In the same circuit (6 ohm parallel with 6 ohm, in series with 3 ohm, 6 V source), the current through each of the parallel resistors is:
mcqs.why: Total current from the source: I = V / Req = 6 / 6.0 = 1.0 A. This divides equally between the two equal parallel resistors, so each carries 1.0 / 2 = 0.5 A, while the full 1.0 A flows through the series resistor.

mcqs.q: A rectangular iron bar is 2.0 cm by 2.0 cm in cross section and 40 cm long. With resistivity of iron 11 x 10^-8 ohm m, its resistance is:
The resistance of an iron wire at 0 degrees C is 1 x 10^4 ohm. With temperature coefficient 5.2 x 10^-3 K^-1, its resistance at 500 degrees C is:
A 24 V cell (internal resistance 0.10 ohm) and a 6.0 V cell (internal resistance 0.90 ohm) oppose each other in a loop with an 8.0 ohm resistor. The loop current is:
mcqs.why: The cells oppose, so the net emf is 24 - 6.0 = 18 V. Total resistance is 0.10 + 8.0 + 0.90 = 9.0 ohm. Loop current I = 18 / 9.0 = 2.0 A.

mcqs.q: In that loop, the 6.0 V cell is being charged by the larger cell. Its terminal potential difference is:
mcqs.why: For a cell being charged, V = E + I r = 6.0 + 2.0 x 0.90 = 6.0 + 1.8 = 7.8 V. (The discharging 24 V cell has V = E - I r = 24 - 2.0 x 0.10 = 23.8 V.)

mcqs.q: A 9.0 V cell forms the left branch of a network; the right branch has a 6.0 V cell in series with a 12 ohm resistor, the cells driving current the same way round the right loop. The current through the 12 ohm resistor is:
mcqs.why: In the right loop the net emf is 9.0 + 6.0 = 15 V, so the current through the 12 ohm resistor is I = 15 / 12 = 1.25 A. (The 18 ohm middle resistor, across 9.0 V, carries 9.0 / 18 = 0.5 A.)

mcqs.q: In a two-loop circuit the left loop current is 0.8 A and the right loop current is 1.4 A; both pass together through a middle 2.0 ohm resistor. The power dissipated in the middle resistor is:
mcqs.why: The middle resistor carries I1 + I2 = 0.8 + 1.4 = 2.2 A. Power P = I^2 R = (2.2)^2 x 2.0 = 4.84 x 2.0 = 9.68 W.

lessons.title: Review Questions
lessons.notes_html:
14.1. A plane conducting loop is located in a uniform magnetic field that is directed along the x-axis. For what orientation of the loop is the flux a maximum? For what orientation is the flux a minimum?

Magnetic flux through the loop is phi = B A cos theta, where theta is the angle between the field and the normal to the plane of the loop.

The flux is a maximum when cos theta = 1, that is, theta = 0.

This happens when the normal to the loop is along the field, so the plane of the loop is perpendicular to the x-axis.

The flux is a minimum, zero, when cos theta = 0, that is, theta = 90 degrees.

This happens when the normal to the loop is perpendicular to the field, so the plane of the loop is parallel to the x-axis.

14.2. A current in a conductor produces a magnetic field, which can be calculated using Ampere's law. Since current is defined as the rate of flow of charge, what can you conclude about the magnetic field due to stationary charges? What about moving charges?

Ampere's law links the magnetic field to the current enclosed, and current is moving charge.

Stationary charges have no current, so they produce no magnetic field at all.

Stationary charges produce only an electric field.

Moving charges, that is, a current, do produce a magnetic field around them.

So magnetism is produced by moving charges, not by charges at rest.

14.3. Describe the change in the magnetic field inside a solenoid carrying a steady current I, if (a) the length of the solenoid is doubled but the number of turns remains the same and (b) the number of turns is doubled, but the length remains the same.

The field inside a solenoid is B = mu-zero n I, where n = N / L is the number of turns per unit length.

(a) Length doubled, turns unchanged: n becomes N / (2L), half its old value.

So the magnetic field is halved.

(b) Turns doubled, length unchanged: n becomes 2N / L, twice its old value.

So the magnetic field is doubled.

14.4. At a given instant, a proton moves in the positive x direction in a region where there is magnetic field in the negative z direction. What is the direction of the magnetic force? Will the proton continue to move in the positive x direction?

Explain.

The magnetic force is F = q v cross B. For a proton q is positive.

Velocity is along +x and the field is along -z, so v cross B is along +y, since x-hat cross (-z-hat) = +y-hat.

So the force on the proton is in the positive y direction.

No, the proton will not continue in the positive x direction.

The force is always perpendicular to its velocity, so it deflects the proton sideways.

The proton moves in a circular path in the x-y plane, its speed staying constant while its direction keeps changing.

14.5. Two charged particles are projected into a region where there is a magnetic field perpendicular to their velocities. If the charges are deflected in opposite directions, what can you say about them?

The magnetic force is F = q v cross B, so its direction depends on the sign of the charge.

Two particles entering with the same velocity direction in the same field feel forces in opposite directions only if their charges have opposite signs.

So one particle is positively charged and the other is negatively charged.

The opposite deflection is the signature of opposite charges.

14.6. Suppose that a charge q is moving in a uniform magnetic field with a velocity v. Why is there no work done by the magnetic force that acts on the charge q?

The magnetic force F = q v cross B is always perpendicular to the velocity v.

The displacement of the charge in any short time is along its velocity.

Work is F dot displacement, and the dot product of perpendicular vectors is zero.

So the magnetic force does no work on the charge.

It changes the direction of motion, but never the speed or the kinetic energy.

14.7. If a charge particle moves in a straight line through some region of space, can you say that the magnetic field in the region is zero?

No, a straight-line path does not prove the field is zero.

If the particle moves parallel to the magnetic field, the angle between v and B is zero, so the magnetic force q v B sin theta is zero.

The particle then goes straight even though a field is present.

Also, an uncharged particle would go straight through any field.

So a straight path alone cannot prove that B is zero.

14.8. Why does the picture on a TV screen become distorted when a magnet is brought near the screen?

A TV picture is made by a beam of electrons striking the screen, and the beam is steered by magnetic fields inside the set.

A magnet brought near the screen adds its own magnetic field in the region of the beam.

This extra field deflects the electrons away from their intended paths.

Electrons then land at the wrong places on the screen, so the picture and colours become distorted.

14.9. Is it possible to orient a current loop in a uniform magnetic field such that the loop will not tend to rotate? Explain.

Yes, it is possible. The torque on a current loop is tau = N I A B sin theta, where theta is the angle between the normal to the loop and the field.

The torque is zero when sin theta = 0, that is, when the normal to the loop is along the field.

This means the plane of the loop is perpendicular to the magnetic field.

In this orientation the loop is in stable equilibrium and has no tendency to rotate.

14.10. How can a current loop be used to determine the presence of a magnetic field in a given region of space?

Place a small current-carrying loop, suspended so it can turn freely, in the region.

If a magnetic field is present, the loop experiences a torque and turns until its plane is perpendicular to the field.

If the loop shows no tendency to turn in any orientation, there is no magnetic field in the region.

The direction in which the loop settles also shows the direction of the field.

So the loop acts as a detector of both the presence and the direction of the field.

14.11. How can you use a magnetic field to separate isotopes of chemical element?

Isotopes of an element have the same charge but different masses.

Give the ions of the element the same kinetic energy, for example by accelerating them through the same potential difference.

Then send them into a uniform magnetic field perpendicular to their motion.

Each ion follows a circular path of radius r = m v / (q B), which depends on its mass.

Heavier isotopes follow larger circles and lighter ones smaller circles, so the isotopes land at different places and are separated.

14.12. What should be the orientation of a current carrying coil in a magnetic field so that torque acting upon the coil is (a) maximum (b) minimum?

The torque on a coil is tau = N I A B sin theta, where theta is the angle between the normal to the coil and the field.

(a) Maximum: sin theta = 1, theta = 90 degrees, so the normal to the coil is perpendicular to the field.

This means the plane of the coil is parallel to the magnetic field.

(b) Minimum: sin theta = 0, theta = 0, so the normal to the coil is along the field.

This means the plane of the coil is perpendicular to the magnetic field, and the torque is zero.

14.13. A loop of wire is suspended between the poles of a magnet with its plane parallel to the pole faces. What happens if a direct current is put through the coil?

What happens if an alternating current is used instead?

With the plane parallel to the pole faces, the plane is parallel to the field, so the torque on the loop is at its maximum.

A direct current gives a steady torque in one direction, so the loop rotates until its plane is perpendicular to the field, where the torque becomes zero, and it settles there.

An alternating current reverses direction every half cycle, so the torque also reverses every half cycle.

The loop therefore cannot rotate steadily; instead it vibrates or oscillates about its mean position.

14.14. Why the resistance of an ammeter should be very low?

An ammeter is connected in series with the circuit whose current is to be measured.

If its resistance were large, it would reduce the current it is trying to measure and change the circuit.

A very low resistance ammeter takes almost no voltage and hardly changes the current.

So the current it reads is very close to the true current in the circuit.

14.15. Why the voltmeter should have a very high resistance?

A voltmeter is connected in parallel across the component whose potential difference is to be measured.

If its resistance were low, it would draw a large current and change the potential difference it is trying to measure.

A very high resistance voltmeter draws almost no current from the circuit.

So it measures the potential difference without disturbing the circuit.

mcqs.q: A plane conducting loop sits in a uniform magnetic field along the x-axis. The magnetic flux through the loop is maximum when:
options: The normal to the loop is along the field, so the plane of the loop is perpendicular to the x-axis
The plane of the loop is parallel to the x-axis
The normal to the loop is perpendicular to the field
The loop is edge-on to the field
mcqs.why: Flux is phi = B A cos theta, where theta is the angle between the field and the normal to the loop. The flux is maximum when cos theta = 1, that is theta = 0: the normal is along the field and the plane of the loop is perpendicular to the x-axis. It is zero when theta = 90 degrees.

mcqs.q: Stationary charges produce:
options: Both an electric and a magnetic field
An electric field only, and no magnetic field
mcqs.why: Ampere's law links the magnetic field to current, and current is moving charge. Stationary charges have no current, so they produce no magnetic field at all; they produce only an electric field. Magnetism is produced by moving charges.

mcqs.q: The length of a solenoid carrying a steady current is doubled while the number of turns stays the same. The magnetic field inside:
mcqs.why: The field inside a solenoid is B = mu-zero n I, with n = N / L. Doubling L with N unchanged halves n, so the magnetic field is halved.

mcqs.q: The number of turns of a solenoid is doubled while its length stays the same. The magnetic field inside:
mcqs.why: With B = mu-zero n I and n = N / L, doubling N at the same L doubles n, so the magnetic field is doubled.

mcqs.q: At a given instant a proton moves in the positive x direction through a magnetic field in the negative z direction. The direction of the magnetic force on the proton is:
mcqs.why: The force is F = q v cross B, and q is positive for a proton. With v along +x and B along -z, v cross B is along +y, because x-hat cross (-z-hat) = +y-hat. So the force is in the positive y direction, and the proton is deflected into a circular path in the x-y plane at constant speed.

mcqs.q: Two charged particles are projected with the same velocity direction into a magnetic field perpendicular to their velocities, and they are deflected in opposite directions. This shows that:
options: They have charges of opposite sign
mcqs.why: The magnetic force F = q v cross B changes direction with the sign of q. Two particles with the same velocity in the same field feel forces in opposite directions only if their charges have opposite signs: one is positive and the other negative.

mcqs.q: A charge moving in a uniform magnetic field feels a magnetic force, yet the force does no work on the charge because:
options: The force is always perpendicular to the velocity, so F dot displacement is zero
The charge moves in a straight line
mcqs.why: The magnetic force F = q v cross B is always perpendicular to the velocity, and the displacement in any short time is along the velocity. The dot product of perpendicular vectors is zero, so no work is done: the force changes the direction of motion but never the speed or kinetic energy.

mcqs.q: A charged particle moves in a straight line through a region of space. Can we conclude that the magnetic field in the region is zero?
options: Yes, a straight path proves B is zero
No, because the electric field cancels it
Yes, because any field would curve the path
No, because a particle moving parallel to the field feels no magnetic force and goes straight
mcqs.why: If the particle moves parallel to the magnetic field, the angle between v and B is zero, so the force q v B sin theta is zero and the particle goes straight even though a field is present. A straight path alone cannot prove that B is zero.

mcqs.q: The torque on a current-carrying coil in a uniform magnetic field is maximum when:
options: The plane of the coil is perpendicular to the field
The normal to the coil is along the field
The plane of the coil is parallel to the field
mcqs.why: The torque is tau = N I A B sin theta, with theta the angle between the normal to the coil and the field. It is maximum when sin theta = 1, theta = 90 degrees: the normal is perpendicular to the field, which means the plane of the coil is parallel to the field. It is minimum (zero) when the plane is perpendicular to the field.

mcqs.q: A magnetic field is used to separate the isotopes of an element because, for ions given the same kinetic energy, the radius of the circular path:
options: Is the same for all isotopes
Depends on the mass, r = m v / (q B), so heavier isotopes follow larger circles
Depends on the colour of the ions
mcqs.why: Isotopes have the same charge but different masses. In a perpendicular magnetic field each ion follows a circle of radius r = m v / (q B), which depends on its mass, so heavier isotopes follow larger circles and lighter ones smaller circles, and they land at different places.

lessons.notes_html:
14.1. Find the value of the magnetic field that will cause a maximum force of 7.0 x 10^-3 N on a 20.0 cm straight wire carrying a current of 10.0 A. (Book answer: 3.5 x 10^-3 T)

Maximum force on a current-carrying wire: F = I L B (when the wire is perpendicular to the field).

So B = F / (I L).

L = 20.0 cm = 0.20 m, I = 10.0 A, F = 7.0 x 10^-3 N.

B = (7.0 x 10^-3) / (10.0 x 0.20) = (7.0 x 10^-3) / 2.0.

Answer: 3.5 x 10^-3 T, as printed in the book.

14.2. How fast must a proton move in a magnetic field of 2.50 x 10^-3 T such that the magnetic force is equal to its weight? (Book answer: 4.09 x 10^-5 m s^-1)

Magnetic force on the proton: F = q v B (motion perpendicular to the field).

Weight of the proton: W = m g.

Set them equal: q v B = m g, so v = m g / (q B).

Mass of proton m = 1.67 x 10^-27 kg, q = 1.60 x 10^-19 C, g = 9.8 m s^-2, B = 2.50 x 10^-3 T. v = (1.67 x 10^-27)(9.8) / ((1.60 x 10^-19)(2.50 x 10^-3)). v = (1.64 x 10^-26) / (4.0 x 10^-22) = 4.09 x 10^-5 m s^-1.

Answer: 4.09 x 10^-5 m s^-1, as printed in the book.

14.3. A velocity selector has a magnetic field of 0.30 T. If a perpendicular electric field of 10,000 V m^-1 is applied, what will be the speed of the particle that will pass through the selector? (Book answer: 3.3 x 10^4 m s^-1)

In a velocity selector the electric and magnetic forces balance: q E = q v B.

So v = E / B. v = 10000 / 0.30 = 33333 m s^-1.

Answer: 3.3 x 10^4 m s^-1, as printed in the book.

14.4. A coil of 0.1 m x 0.1 m and of 200 turns carrying a current of 1.0 mA is placed in a uniform magnetic field of 0.1 T. Calculate the maximum torque that acts on the coil. (Book answer: 2.0 x 10^-4 N m)

Area of the coil: A = 0.1 x 0.1 = 0.01 m squared.

Maximum torque: tau = N I A B (when sin theta = 1). tau = 200 x (1.0 x 10^-3) x 0.01 x 0.1. tau = 200 x 1.0 x 10^-6 = 2.0 x 10^-4 N m.

Answer: 2.0 x 10^-4 N m, as printed in the book.

14.5. A power line 10.0 m high carries a current 200 A. Find the magnetic field of the wire at the ground. (Book answer: 4.0 x 10^-6 T)

Field of a long straight wire: B = (mu-zero I) / (2 pi r).

Here I = 200 A and r = 10.0 m (the height of the line above the ground).

B = (4 pi x 10^-7 x 200) / (2 pi x 10.0).

B = (2 x 10^-7 x 200) / 10.0 = 4.0 x 10^-6 T.

Answer: 4.0 x 10^-6 T, as printed in the book.

14.6. You are asked to design a solenoid that will give a magnetic field of 0.10 T, yet the current must not exceed 10.0 A. Find the number of turns per unit length that the solenoid should have. (Book answer: 7.96 x 10^3)

Field of a solenoid: B = mu-zero n I, where n is turns per unit length.

So n = B / (mu-zero I). n = 0.10 / ((4 pi x 10^-7) x 10.0). n = 0.10 / (1.256 x 10^-5) = 7960.

Answer: 7.96 x 10^3 turns per metre, as printed in the book.

14.7. What current should pass through a solenoid that is 0.5 m long with 10,000 turns of copper wire so that it will have a magnetic field of 0.4 T? (Book answer: 16.0 A)

Field of a solenoid: B = mu-zero (N / L) I.

So I = B L / (mu-zero N).

I = (0.4 x 0.5) / ((4 pi x 10^-7) x 10000).

I = 0.20 / 0.01256 = 15.9 A.

Answer: 16.0 A, as printed in the book.

14.8. A galvanometer having an internal resistance Rg = 15.0 ohm gives full scale deflection with current Ig = 20.0 mA. It is to be converted into an ammeter of range 10.0 A. Find the value of shunt resistance Rs. (Book answer: 0.030 ohm)

The shunt is connected in parallel with the galvanometer, so the voltage across both is the same.

Ig Rg = (I - Ig) Rs, so Rs = Ig Rg / (I - Ig).

Ig = 20.0 mA = 0.020 A, Rg = 15.0 ohm, I = 10.0 A.

Rs = (0.020 x 15.0) / (10.0 - 0.020) = 0.30 / 9.98.

Answer: 0.030 ohm, as printed in the book.

14.9. The resistance of a galvanometer is 50.0 ohm and reads full scale deflection with a current of 2.0 mA. Show by a diagram how to convert this galvanometer into voltmeter reading 200 V full scale. (Book answer: Rh = 99950 ohm)

To convert a galvanometer into a voltmeter, a high resistance Rh is connected in SERIES with it, as in the diagram: galvanometer - Rh - in series across the points whose potential difference is measured.

At full scale the current through the series combination is Ig = 2.0 mA = 0.002 A and the voltage across it is V = 200 V.

Total resistance needed: R = V / Ig = 200 / 0.002 = 100000 ohm.

So Rh = R - Rg = 100000 - 50.

Answer: Rh = 99950 ohm, as printed in the book.

14.10. The resistance of a galvanometer coil is 10.0 ohm and reads full scale with a current of 1.0 mA. What should be the values of resistances R1, R2 and R3 to convert this galvanometer into a multirange ammeter of 100, 10.0 and 1.0 A as shown in the Fig. P. 14.10? (Book answers: R1 = 0.0001 ohm, R2 = 0.001 ohm, R3 = 0.01 ohm)

In Fig. P. 14.10 the galvanometer (Rg = 10.0 ohm, Ig = 1.0 mA = 0.001 A) is fitted with a shunt for each range, with taps at 100 A, 10 A and 1 A.

For a range I, the shunt Rs satisfies Ig Rg = (I - Ig) Rs, so Rs = Ig Rg / (I - Ig).

Ig Rg = 0.001 x 10.0 = 0.01 V.

100 A range: R1 = 0.01 / (100 - 0.001) = 0.0001 ohm.

10 A range: R2 = 0.01 / (10.0 - 0.001) = 0.001 ohm.

1.0 A range: R3 = 0.01 / (1.0 - 0.001) = 0.01 ohm.

Answers: R1 = 0.0001 ohm, R2 = 0.001 ohm, R3 = 0.01 ohm, as printed in the book.

lessons.title: Review Questions
lessons.notes_html:
15.1. Does the induced emf in a circuit depend on the resistance of the circuit? Does the induced current depend on the resistance of the circuit?

The induced emf does NOT depend on the resistance of the circuit.

By Faraday's law, emf = -N (change in flux) / (change in time); it depends only on how fast the magnetic flux changes.

The induced current DOES depend on the resistance.

By Ohm's law, induced current = induced emf / resistance, so a larger resistance gives a smaller induced current for the same emf.

15.2. A square loop of wire is moving through a uniform magnetic field. The normal to the loop is oriented parallel to the magnetic field. Is a emf induced in the loop?

Give a reason for your answer.

No, no emf is induced in the loop.

The flux through the loop is phi = B A, since the normal is parallel to the field and the field is uniform.

As the loop moves wholly inside the uniform field, neither B, nor the area, nor the orientation changes.

So the flux stays constant, its rate of change is zero, and by Faraday's law no emf is induced.

15.3. A light metallic ring is released from above into a vertical bar magnet (Fig. Q. 15.3). Viewed for above, does the current flow clockwise or anticlockwise in the ring?

Viewed from above, the current flows CLOCKWISE in the ring.

The ring falls towards the north pole of the magnet, so the upward magnetic flux through the ring increases as it approaches.

By Lenz's law, the induced current opposes this increase by creating a magnetic field pointing downward through the ring.

A clockwise current, viewed from above, produces a field pointing downward through the ring.

So the induced current is clockwise when viewed from above.

15.4. What is the direction of the current through resistor R in Fig. Q. 15.4? When switch S is (a) closed (b) opened. (Fig: primary coil with battery and switch S on the left, secondary coil with resistor R on the right, both coils wound the same way.)

When the switch is closed, current builds up in the primary and its magnetic field through the secondary grows, pointing to the right.

By Lenz's law the secondary current opposes this growth by making a field pointing to the left.

With the winding as drawn, that secondary current flows through resistor R from LEFT to RIGHT.

(a) Switch closed: current through R flows from left to right, while the primary field is building up.

When the switch is opened, the primary field to the right collapses.

The secondary current now opposes the decrease by making a field pointing to the right, the same way as the primary field did.

(b) Switch opened: current through R flows from right to left.

15.5. Does the induced emf always act to decrease the magnetic flux through a circuit?

No, the induced emf does not always act to decrease the flux.

Lenz's law says the induced emf opposes the CHANGE in flux, not the flux itself.

If the flux is increasing, the induced emf acts to decrease it.

But if the flux is decreasing, the induced emf acts to increase it, that is, to sustain it.

So the induced emf always fights the change, whichever way the flux is changing.

15.6. When the switch in the circuit is closed a current is established in the coil and the metal ring jumps upward (Fig. Q. 15.6). Why? Describe what would happen to the ring if the battery polarity were reversed?

Closing the switch makes the current, and hence the magnetic flux through the ring, grow rapidly.

By Lenz's law the ring carries an induced current whose magnetic field opposes the growth of the coil's field.

The ring's field and the coil's field repel each other, so the ring is pushed upward and jumps.

If the battery polarity were reversed, the coil's field would point the other way, but it would still be growing when the switch is closed.

The induced current would again oppose the growth, so the ring would STILL jump upward.

Reversing the polarity does not stop the jump; repulsion happens for either polarity.

15.7. The Fig. Q. 15.7 shows a coil of wire in the xy plane with a magnetic field directed along the y-axis. Around which of the three coordinate axes should the coil be rotated in order to generate an emf and a current in the coil?

The coil should be rotated about the x-axis.

The coil lies in the xy plane, so its normal is along the z-axis, perpendicular to the field along y, and the initial flux is zero.

Rotating about the x-axis tips the normal towards the y-axis, so the flux through the coil changes from zero to a growing value.

A changing flux induces an emf and a current.

Rotating about the y-axis keeps the normal perpendicular to the field, and rotating about the z-axis spins the coil in its own plane; in both cases the flux stays zero and no emf is generated.

15.8. How would you position a flat loop of wire in a changing magnetic field so that there is no emf induced in the loop?

Position the loop so that its plane is parallel to the magnetic field.

Then the normal to the loop is perpendicular to the field, so cos theta = 0 and the flux through the loop is zero.

Even though the field strength is changing, the flux stays zero at all times.

With no change in flux, Faraday's law gives no induced emf.

15.9. In a certain region the earth's magnetic field point vertically down. When a plane flies due north, which wingtip is positively charged?

The west wingtip, the left wingtip as seen by a pilot facing north, becomes positively charged.

The free charges in the wing move north with the plane through a field pointing down.

The magnetic force q v cross B pushes positive charges towards the west and electrons towards the east.

So positive charge collects on the west (left) wingtip and the east (right) wingtip becomes negatively charged.

15.10. Show that epsilon and (change in flux) / (change in time) have the same units.

Faraday's law says emf = -N (change in flux) / (change in time), so the two sides must have the same units.

The unit of magnetic flux is the weber: 1 Wb = 1 T m squared.

Since 1 T = 1 N / (A m), we get 1 Wb = 1 N m / A = 1 J / A.

Dividing by time: 1 Wb / s = 1 J / (A s) = 1 J / C.

But 1 volt = 1 J / C, so 1 Wb / s = 1 V.

Hence (change in flux) / (change in time) has the unit volt, the same as emf.

15.11. When an electric motor, such as an electric drill, is being used, does it also act as a generator? If so what is the consequence of this?

Yes, a running motor also acts as a generator.

Its coil rotates in a magnetic field, so by electromagnetic induction an emf, the back emf, is induced in the coil.

The back emf opposes the supply voltage, so the net voltage driving current is supply voltage minus back emf.

As the motor speeds up, the back emf grows and the current drawn falls.

This is why a motor draws a large current at start-up, when it is not yet turning, and a much smaller current at full speed.

15.12. Can a D.C motor be turned into a D.C generator? What changes are required to be done?

Yes, a D.C. motor and a D.C. generator have the same construction; either can do the other's job.

To turn the motor into a generator, remove the supply battery and connect a load across its terminals instead.

Drive the shaft mechanically with an external prime mover, such as an engine or a turbine, instead of feeding it current.

The rotating coil then cuts the magnetic field and generates an emf, and the split-ring commutator delivers it as direct current.

No change to the coil, magnet or commutator is needed.

15.13. Is it possible to change both the area of the loop and the magnetic field passing through the loop and still not have an induced emf in the loop?

Yes, it is possible, provided the magnetic flux stays constant.

Flux is phi = B A cos theta, so if B increases while A decreases in the same proportion, the product B A stays the same.

With the flux unchanged, its rate of change is zero.

So by Faraday's law no emf is induced, even though both B and A are changing.

15.14. Can an electric motor be used to drive an electric generator with the output from the generator being used to operate the motor?

No, such a self-running combination cannot work.

The generator's output is always less than the energy fed into it, because of friction, resistance heating and other losses.

If the generator fed the motor, the motor would get back less energy than it spent driving the generator.

The system would slow down and stop; it cannot sustain itself.

This would be a perpetual-motion machine, which the law of conservation of energy forbids.

15.15. A suspended magnet is oscillating freely in a horizontal plane. The oscillations are strongly damped when a metal plate is placed under the magnet. Explain why this occurs?

The oscillating magnet's changing magnetic flux through the metal plate induces eddy currents in the plate.

By Lenz's law, these eddy currents create magnetic fields that oppose the magnet's motion.

The opposing force drains the magnet's energy, which is dissipated as heat in the plate.

So the oscillations die away quickly: this is electromagnetic damping.

15.16. Four unmarked wires emerge from a transformer. What steps would you take to determine the turns ratio?

Step 1: Identify the two windings. Use a continuity tester or ohmmeter: the two wires of one winding show continuity with each other and a low resistance, while wires of different windings show no continuity.

Step 2: Label one winding as primary and the other as secondary.

Step 3: Apply a known alternating voltage to the primary winding and measure the voltage across the secondary winding with a voltmeter.

Step 4: The turns ratio is Ns / Np = Vs / Vp, the ratio of the measured secondary voltage to the applied primary voltage.

The winding with the higher voltage has the larger number of turns.

15.17. a) Can a step-up transformer increase the power level? b) In a transformer, there is no transfer of charge from the primary to the secondary. How is, then the power transferred?

(a) No, a step-up transformer cannot increase the power level.

For an ideal transformer, power out equals power in: Vs Is = Vp Ip.

Raising the voltage lowers the current in the same proportion, so the power stays the same, and in a real transformer it is slightly less because of losses.

(b) Power is transferred by the changing magnetic flux in the core, not by charge crossing over.

The alternating primary current creates a changing flux in the iron core.

This changing flux links the secondary coil and induces an emf in it, delivering power to the secondary circuit.

So energy flows through the magnetic field of the core, with no charge passing from primary to secondary.

15.18. When the primary of a transformer is connected to a.c mains the current in it a) is very small if the secondary circuit is open, but b) increases when the secondary circuit is closed. Explain these facts.

(a) Secondary open: no secondary current flows, so there is no secondary flux to oppose the primary flux.

The primary then needs only a small magnetizing current to set up the core flux, plus a little for core losses, so the primary current is very small.

(b) Secondary closed: the secondary current creates a flux that opposes the primary flux, by Lenz's law.

To keep the core flux at the value set by the mains voltage, the primary must draw extra current to cancel this opposing flux.

So the primary current increases, roughly in proportion to the load on the secondary.

mcqs.q: Does the induced emf in a circuit depend on the resistance of the circuit? Does the induced current?
options: The emf does not depend on the resistance, but the induced current does
The emf depends on the resistance, but the current does not

mcqs.q: A square loop of wire moves wholly inside a uniform magnetic field, its normal parallel to the field. The emf induced in the loop is:
options: Maximum, because the flux is maximum
Zero, because the flux stays constant as the loop moves
Alternating, because the loop is moving
mcqs.why: The flux through the loop is phi = B A and stays constant while the loop moves wholly inside the uniform field: neither B, nor the area, nor the orientation changes. With no change of flux, Faraday's law gives no induced emf.

mcqs.q: According to Lenz's law, the induced emf always acts to:
options: Decrease the magnetic flux through the circuit
Increase the magnetic flux through the circuit
Oppose the change in magnetic flux through the circuit
Keep the current in the circuit constant
mcqs.why: Lenz's law says the induced emf opposes the CHANGE in flux, not the flux itself. If the flux is increasing it acts to decrease it, but if the flux is decreasing it acts to increase it, that is, to sustain it.

mcqs.q: When the switch of a coil circuit is closed, a metal ring above the coil jumps upward. If the battery polarity is reversed and the switch is closed again, the ring:
options: Is pulled down onto the coil
mcqs.why: Closing the switch makes the flux through the ring grow rapidly whichever way the coil's field points. By Lenz's law the ring's induced current opposes the growth, the two fields repel, and the ring is pushed upward. Reversing the polarity reverses both fields, so the repulsion, and the jump, still happen.

mcqs.q: A coil of wire lies in the xy plane with a magnetic field directed along the y-axis. To generate an emf in the coil, it should be rotated about:
options: Any axis; rotation always induces an emf
mcqs.why: The coil's normal is along z, perpendicular to the field along y, so the flux is initially zero. Rotating about the x-axis tips the normal towards the y-axis, so the flux changes and an emf is induced. Rotating about y or z keeps the flux at zero, so no emf is generated.

mcqs.q: How should a flat loop be positioned in a changing magnetic field so that no emf is induced in it?
options: With its plane perpendicular to the field
With its plane parallel to the field, so the flux through it stays zero
With its normal along the field
It is impossible; a changing field always induces an emf
mcqs.why: With the plane of the loop parallel to the field, the normal is perpendicular to the field and cos theta = 0, so the flux through the loop is zero at all times. Even though the field strength changes, there is no change in flux, so no emf is induced.

mcqs.q: In a region where the earth's magnetic field points vertically down, a plane flies due north. Which wingtip becomes positively charged?
mcqs.why: The free charges in the wing move north through a downward field. The magnetic force q v cross B pushes positive charges towards the west and electrons towards the east, so the west (left) wingtip becomes positively charged and the east wingtip negatively charged.

mcqs.q: A running electric motor also acts as a generator. The consequence is that:
options: It produces a back emf opposing the supply, so it draws a large current at start-up and a smaller current at full speed
It charges the supply battery while running
Its current increases as it speeds up
It needs no supply once started
mcqs.why: The rotating coil cuts the magnetic field and an emf, the back emf, is induced in it, opposing the supply voltage. The net driving voltage is supply minus back emf; as the motor speeds up the back emf grows and the current falls. At start-up there is no back emf, so the current is large.

options: Yes, power rises with the voltage
No, for an ideal transformer power out equals power in; raising the voltage lowers the current in the same proportion
Yes, if the core is laminated
No, because a transformer lowers the voltage
mcqs.why: For an ideal transformer Vs Is = Vp Ip: the power stays the same, and in a real transformer it is slightly less because of losses. Power is transferred by the changing magnetic flux in the core, not by charge crossing from primary to secondary.
