15.1. An emf of 0.45 V is induced between the ends of a metal bar moving through a magnetic field of 0.22 T. What field strength would be needed to produce an emf of 1.5 V between the ends of the bar, assuming that all other factors remain the same? (Book answer: 0.73 T)

Motional emf is proportional to the field: emf is proportional to B, all else unchanged.

So B2 / B1 = emf2 / emf1.

B2 = 0.22 x (1.5 / 0.45).

B2 = 0.22 x 3.333 = 0.733.

Answer: 0.73 T, as printed in the book.

15.2. The flux density B in a region between the pole faces of a horse-shoe magnet is 0.5 Wb m^-2 directed vertically downward. Find the emf induced in a straight wire 5.0 cm long, perpendicular to B when it is moved in a direction at an angle of 60 degrees with the horizontal with a speed of 100 cm s^-1. (Book answer: 1.25 x 10^-2 V)

Motional emf: emf = B L v-perpendicular, where v-perpendicular is the velocity component perpendicular to the field.

The wire moves at 60 degrees to the horizontal, and the field is vertical, so the horizontal velocity component is perpendicular to the field.

Horizontal component: v cos 60 degrees = 100 cm s^-1 x 0.5 = 50 cm s^-1 = 0.50 m s^-1.

Length: L = 5.0 cm = 0.050 m, B = 0.5 T. emf = 0.5 x 0.050 x 0.50 = 0.0125 V.

Answer: 1.25 x 10^-2 V, as printed in the book.

15.3. A coil of wire has 10 loops. Each loop has an area of 1.5 x 10^-3 m squared. A magnetic field is perpendicular to the surface of each loop at all times. If the magnetic field is changed from 0.05 T to 0.06 T in 0.1 s, find the average emf induced in the coil during this time. (Book answer: +1.5 x 10^-3 V)

Faraday's law: emf = N A (change in B) / (change in time).

Change in B = 0.06 - 0.05 = 0.01 T. Time = 0.1 s. N = 10, A = 1.5 x 10^-3 m squared. emf = 10 x (1.5 x 10^-3) x 0.01 / 0.1. emf = 10 x (1.5 x 10^-3) x 0.1 = 1.5 x 10^-3 V.

Answer: +1.5 x 10^-3 V, as printed in the book (the positive sign follows the book's sign convention).

15.4. A circular coil has 15 turns of radius 2 cm each. The plane of the coil lies at 40 degrees to a uniform magnetic field of 0.2 T. If the field is increased by 0.5 T in 0.2 s, find the magnitude of the induced emf. (Book answer: 1.8 x 10^-2 V - see note)

Step 1: Area of one turn: A = pi r squared = pi x (0.02) squared = 1.26 x 10^-3 m squared.

Step 2: The plane is at 40 degrees to the field, so the normal to the coil is at 50 degrees to the field, and cos 50 degrees = 0.643.

Step 3: Rate of change of field from the stem as printed: change in B / change in time = 0.5 / 0.2 = 2.5 T s^-1.

Step 4: emf = N A cos 50 degrees x (change in B / change in time). emf = 15 x (1.26 x 10^-3) x 0.643 x 2.5 = 3.0 x 10^-2 V.

NOTE ON THE PRINTED ANSWER: the book prints 1.8 x 10^-2 V, which is the value obtained if the field change is 0.3 T, that is, the field rising FROM 0.2 T TO 0.5 T (0.5 - 0.2 = 0.3): 15 x (1.26 x 10^-3) x 0.643 x (0.3 / 0.2) = 1.8 x 10^-2 V. The step-by-step value from the stem as printed ('increased by 0.5 T') is 3.0 x 10^-2 V; the book's printed 1.8 x 10^-2 V is recorded here as printed, not silently substituted.

15.5. Two coils are placed side by side. An emf of 0.8 V is observed in one coil when the current is changing at the rate of 200 A s^-1 in the other coil. What is the mutual inductance of the coils? (Book answer: 4 mH)

Mutual induction: emf = M x (rate of change of current).

So M = emf / (rate of change of current).

M = 0.8 / 200 = 0.004 H.

Answer: 4 mH, as printed in the book.

15.6. A pair of adjacent coils has a mutual inductance of 0.75 H. If the current in the primary changes from 0 to 10 A in 0.025 s, what is the average induced emf in the secondary? What is the change in flux in it if the secondary has 500 turns? (Book answers: 300 V, 1.5 x 10^-2 Wb)

Step 1: Average induced emf: emf = M (change in I) / (change in time). emf = 0.75 x (10 - 0) / 0.025 = 0.75 x 400 = 300 V.

Step 2: For the secondary, emf = N (change in flux) / (change in time), so change in flux = emf x (change in time) / N.

Change in flux = 300 x 0.025 / 500 = 7.5 / 500 = 0.015 Wb.

Answers: 300 V and 1.5 x 10^-2 Wb, as printed in the book.

15.7. A solenoid has 250 turns and its self inductance is 2.4 mH. What is the flux through each turn when the current is 2 A? What is the induced emf when the current changes at 20 A s^-1? (Book answers: 1.92 x 10^-5 Wb, 48 mV)

Step 1: Self inductance: L = N flux / I, so flux = L I / N.

Flux = (2.4 x 10^-3) x 2 / 250 = 4.8 x 10^-3 / 250.

Flux = 1.92 x 10^-5 Wb.

Step 2: Induced emf: emf = L (change in I) / (change in time). emf = (2.4 x 10^-3) x 20 = 0.048 V.

Answers: 1.92 x 10^-5 Wb and 48 mV, as printed in the book.

15.8. A solenoid of length 8.0 cm and cross sectional area 0.5 cm squared has 520 turns. Find the self inductance of the solenoid when the core is air. If the current in the solenoid increases through 1.5 A in 0.2 s, find the magnitude of induced emf in it. (mu-zero = 4 pi x 10^-7 Wb A^-1 m^-1) (Book answers: 1.6 x 10^-3 V, 2.12 x 10^-4 H)

Step 1: Self inductance of a solenoid: L = mu-zero N squared A / l.

N squared = 520 squared = 270400. A = 0.5 cm squared = 0.5 x 10^-4 m squared. l = 8.0 cm = 0.080 m.

L = (4 pi x 10^-7) x 270400 x (0.5 x 10^-4) / 0.080.

L = 2.12 x 10^-4 H.

Step 2: Induced emf: emf = L (change in I) / (change in time). emf = (2.12 x 10^-4) x 1.5 / 0.2 = (2.12 x 10^-4) x 7.5. emf = 1.6 x 10^-3 V.

Answers: 1.6 x 10^-3 V and 2.12 x 10^-4 H, as printed in the book.

15.9. When current through a coil changes from 100 mA to 200 mA in 0.005 s, an induced emf of 40 mV is produced in the coil. (a) What is the self inductance of the coil? (b) Find the increase in the energy stored in the coil. (Book answers: 2 mH, 0.03 mJ)

Step 1: (a) emf = L (change in I) / (change in time), so L = emf x (change in time) / (change in I).

Change in I = 200 - 100 = 100 mA = 0.100 A. emf = 40 mV = 0.040 V.

L = 0.040 x 0.005 / 0.100 = 0.002 H.

Step 2: (b) Energy stored: U = (1/2) L I squared. Increase = (1/2) L (I2 squared - I1 squared).

Increase = 0.5 x 0.002 x ((0.200) squared - (0.100) squared).

Increase = 0.001 x (0.040 - 0.010) = 0.001 x 0.030 = 3.0 x 10^-5 J.

Answers: 2 mH and 0.03 mJ, as printed in the book.

15.10. Like any field, the earth's magnetic field stores energy. Find the magnetic energy stored in a space where strength of earth's field is 7 x 10^-5 T, if the space occupies an area of 10 x 10^8 m squared and has a height of 750 m.

(Book answer: 1.46 x 10^9 J)

Step 1: Energy density in a magnetic field: u = B squared / (2 mu-zero). u = (7 x 10^-5) squared / (2 x 4 pi x 10^-7) = (49 x 10^-10) / (2.51 x 10^-6). u = 1.95 x 10^-3 J m^-3.

Step 2: Volume: V = area x height = (10 x 10^8) x 750 = 7.5 x 10^11 m cubed.

Step 3: Total energy: U = u V = (1.95 x 10^-3) x (7.5 x 10^11).

U = 1.46 x 10^9 J.

Answer: 1.46 x 10^9 J, as printed in the book.

15.11. A square coil of side 16 cm has 200 turns and rotates in a uniform magnetic field of magnitude 0.05 T. If the peak emf is 12 V, what is the angular velocity of the coil (Book answer: 47 rad s^-1)

Peak emf of a rotating coil: emf-zero = N A B omega.

Area: A = 0.16 x 0.16 = 0.0256 m squared.

So omega = emf-zero / (N A B) = 12 / (200 x 0.0256 x 0.05). omega = 12 / 0.256 = 46.9 rad s^-1.

Answer: 47 rad s^-1, as printed in the book.

15.12. A generator has a rectangular coil consisting of 360 turns. The coil rotates at 420 rev per min in 0.14 T magnetic field. The peak value of emf produced by the generator is 50 V. If the coil is 5.0 cm wide, find the length of the side of the coil. (Book answer: 45 cm)

Step 1: Frequency: f = 420 / 60 = 7 rev s^-1. Angular velocity: omega = 2 pi f = 2 pi x 7 = 44.0 rad s^-1.

Step 2: Peak emf: emf-zero = N A B omega, so A = emf-zero / (N B omega).

A = 50 / (360 x 0.14 x 44.0) = 50 / 2218 = 0.0225 m squared.

Step 3: Area = width x length, so length = A / width = 0.0225 / 0.050.

Length = 0.45 m.

Answer: 45 cm, as printed in the book.

15.13. It is desired to make an a.c generator that can produce an emf of maximum value 5 kV with 50 Hz frequency. A coil of area 1 m squared having 200 turns is used as armature. What should be the magnitude of the magnetic field in which the coil rotates? (Book answer: 0.08 T)

Peak emf: emf-zero = N A B omega, with omega = 2 pi f. omega = 2 pi x 50 = 314 rad s^-1.

So B = emf-zero / (N A omega) = 5000 / (200 x 1 x 314).

B = 5000 / 62800 = 0.0796 T.

Answer: 0.08 T, as printed in the book.

15.14. The back emf in a motor is 120 V when the motor is turning at 1680 rev per min. What is the back emf when the motor turns 3360 rev per min? (Book answer: 240 V)

Back emf is proportional to the speed of rotation.

So emf2 / emf1 = speed2 / speed1 = 3360 / 1680 = 2. emf2 = 120 x 2 = 240 V.

Answer: 240 V, as printed in the book.

15.15. A D.C motor operates at 240 V and has a resistance of 0.5 ohm.

When the motor is running at normal speed, the armature current is 15 A. Find the back emf in the armature. (Book answer: 232.5 V) For a motor: supply voltage V = back emf + I R.

So back emf = V - I R.

Back emf = 240 - (15 x 0.5) = 240 - 7.5.

Answer: 232.5 V, as printed in the book.

15.16. A copper ring has a radius of 4.0 cm and resistance of 1.0 m ohm. A magnetic field is applied over the ring, perpendicular to its plane. If the magnetic field increases from 0.2 T to 0.4 T in a time interval of 5 x 10^-3 s, what is the current in the ring during this interval? (Book answer: 201 A)

Step 1: Area of the ring: A = pi r squared = pi x (0.040) squared = 5.03 x 10^-3 m squared.

Step 2: Induced emf: emf = A (change in B) / (change in time). emf = (5.03 x 10^-3) x (0.4 - 0.2) / (5 x 10^-3) = (5.03 x 10^-3) x 40. emf = 0.201 V.

Step 3: Current: I = emf / R, with R = 1.0 m ohm = 1.0 x 10^-3 ohm.

I = 0.201 / (1.0 x 10^-3) = 201 A.

Answer: 201 A, as printed in the book.

15.17. A coil of 10 turns and 35 cm squared area is in a perpendicular magnetic field of 0.5 T. The coil is pulled out of the field in 1.0 s. Find the induced emf in the coil as it is pulled out of the field. (Book answer: 1.75 x 10^-2 V)

Flux through the coil falls from B A to zero in 1.0 s. emf = N A B / time.

A = 35 cm squared = 35 x 10^-4 m squared. emf = 10 x (35 x 10^-4) x 0.5 / 1.0 = 10 x 0.0035 x 0.5.

Answer: 1.75 x 10^-2 V, as printed in the book.

15.18. An ideal step down transformer is connected to main supply of 240 V. It is desired to operate a 12 V, 30 W lamp. Find the current in the primary and the transformation ratio? (Book answers: 0.125 A, 1/20)

Step 1: For an ideal transformer, power in = power out = 30 W.

Primary current: Ip = P / Vp = 30 / 240 = 0.125 A.

Step 2: Transformation ratio: Ns / Np = Vs / Vp = 12 / 240.

Ratio = 1 / 20.

Answers: 0.125 A and 1/20, as printed in the book. (Secondary current, for reference, is 30 / 12 = 2.5 A.)

lessons.title: Review Questions
lessons.notes_html:
16.1. A sinusoidal current has rms value of 10 A. What is the maximum or peak value?

For a sinusoidal current, the rms value is the peak value divided by the square root of 2: I-rms = I-zero / sqrt(2).

So the peak value is I-zero = I-rms x sqrt(2).

I-zero = 10 x 1.414 = 14.14 A.

Answer: the maximum or peak value is about 14.1 A.

16.2. Name the device that will (a) permit flow of direct current but oppose the flow of alternating current (b) permit flow of alternating current but not the direct current.

(a) An inductor, or choke coil, permits direct current but opposes alternating current.

Its inductive reactance is X-L = 2 pi f L. For direct current f = 0, so X-L = 0 and the current passes freely.

For alternating current f is not zero, so X-L opposes the current.

(b) A capacitor permits alternating current but not direct current.

Its capacitive reactance is X-C = 1 / (2 pi f C). For direct current f = 0, so X-C is infinite and no steady current passes.

For alternating current X-C is finite, so the current passes.

16.3. How many times per second will an incandescent lamp reach maximum brilliance when connected to a 50 Hz source?

The brilliance of the lamp follows the power, which follows the square of the current.

In one cycle of a 50 Hz supply, the current reaches its positive peak once and its negative peak once.

The square of the current, and hence the brilliance, is a maximum at both peaks.

So the lamp reaches maximum brilliance twice per cycle.

Answer: 2 x 50 = 100 times per second.

16.4. A circuit contains an iron-cored inductor, a switch and a D.C. source arranged in series. The switch is closed and after an interval reopened. Explain why a spark jumps across the switch contacts?

While the switch is closed, a steady current flows and the inductor stores energy in its magnetic field.

When the switch is reopened, the current tries to fall to zero suddenly, so the rate of change of current is very large.

The inductor opposes this change by inducing a very large emf, emf = -L (change in current) / (change in time).

This large induced emf appears across the opening switch contacts.

It is high enough to break down the air gap, ionize it, and a spark jumps across the contacts.

16.5. How does doubling the frequency affect the reactance of (a) an inductor (b) a capacitor?

(a) Inductor: X-L = 2 pi f L, so reactance is directly proportional to frequency.

Doubling the frequency doubles the inductive reactance.

(b) Capacitor: X-C = 1 / (2 pi f C), so reactance is inversely proportional to frequency.

Doubling the frequency halves the capacitive reactance.

16.6. In a R - L circuit, will the current lag or lead the voltage? Illustrate your answer by a vector diagram.

In an R-L circuit the current LAGS the voltage.

The voltage across the resistor, V-R, is in phase with the current I.

The voltage across the inductor, V-L, leads the current by 90 degrees, because the inductor opposes changes in current.

Vector diagram: draw the current vector I as the reference along the horizontal.

Draw V-R along I, and V-L 90 degrees ahead of (above) I.

The total applied voltage V is the vector sum of V-R and V-L, and it lies ahead of I by the phase angle phi, where tan phi = X-L / R.

So the current lags behind the applied voltage by phi.

16.7. A choke coil placed in series with an electric lamp in an A.C. circuit causes the lamp to become dim. Why is it so? A variable capacitor added in series in this circuit may be adjusted until the lamp glows with normal brilliance. Explain, how this is possible?

The choke coil adds inductive reactance X-L to the circuit, so the total impedance Z becomes larger.

A larger impedance means a smaller current, so the lamp, which now gets less current, becomes dim.

Adding a variable capacitor in series adds capacitive reactance X-C, which subtracts from X-L in the impedance.

By adjusting the capacitance until X-C = X-L, the circuit reaches resonance.

At resonance the impedance is at its minimum, equal to the resistance alone, so the current is at its maximum.

The lamp then gets its full current again and glows with normal brilliance.

16.8. Explain the conditions under which electromagnetic waves are produced from a source?

Electromagnetic waves are produced by accelerating electric charges.

A charge oscillating back and forth, for example in a transmitting antenna, creates a changing electric field.

The changing electric field creates a changing magnetic field, which in turn creates a changing electric field, and so on.

These mutually sustaining changing fields detach from the source and travel outwards through space.

No medium is needed: the waves propagate even through vacuum at the speed of light.

16.9. How the reception of a particular radio station is selected on your radio set?

The radio set has a tuning circuit, a coil and a variable capacitor in parallel, with a natural resonant frequency f = 1 / (2 pi sqrt(L C)).

By turning the tuning knob, the capacitance is changed until the circuit's resonant frequency equals the carrier frequency of the wanted station.

At resonance, that station's signal builds up a large response in the circuit, while other stations, off resonance, give only a tiny response.

So the wanted station is selected and the others are rejected.

16.10. What is meant by A.M. and F.M.?

A.M. means amplitude modulation. The amplitude of a high-frequency carrier wave is varied in step with the low-frequency signal, while the carrier frequency stays constant.

F.M. means frequency modulation. The frequency of the carrier wave is varied in step with the signal, while the carrier amplitude stays constant.

In both cases the signal is carried by the modulated carrier wave to the receiver, which recovers the original signal.

At the setting where X-C = X-L the circuit is at resonance, the impedance is minimum and the current is maximum
The capacitor removes the resistance of the choke
The capacitor increases the supply voltage

The frequency of the carrier is varied in step with the signal, amplitude constant
Both amplitude and frequency of the carrier are varied
The signal replaces the carrier wave

lessons.title: Numerical Problems - Worked in Full
lessons.notes_html:
16.1. An alternating current is represented by the equation I = 20 sin 100 pi t. Compute its frequency and the maximum and rms values of current. (Book answers: 50 Hz, 20 A, 14 A)

Compare with I = I-zero sin (omega t): omega = 100 pi.

Frequency: f = omega / (2 pi) = 100 pi / (2 pi) = 50 Hz.

Maximum value: I-zero = 20 A. rms value: I-rms = I-zero / sqrt(2) = 20 / 1.414 = 14.14 A.

Answers: 50 Hz, 20 A, 14 A, as printed in the book.

16.2. A sinusoidal A.C. has a maximum value of 15 A. What are its rms values? If the time is recorded from the instant the current is zero and is becoming positive, what is the instantaneous value of the current after 1 / 300 s, given the frequency is 50 Hz. (Book answers: I-rms = 10.6 A, Instantaneous current = 13.0 A)

Step 1: rms value: I-rms = I-zero / sqrt(2) = 15 / 1.414 = 10.6 A.

Step 2: Instantaneous current: I = I-zero sin (omega t), with omega = 2 pi f = 2 pi x 50 = 100 pi rad s^-1.

At t = 1 / 300 s: omega t = 100 pi / 300 = pi / 3 = 60 degrees.

I = 15 x sin 60 degrees = 15 x 0.866 = 13.0 A.

Answers: I-rms = 10.6 A and instantaneous current = 13.0 A, as printed in the book.

16.3. Find the value of the current and inductive reactance when A.C.

voltage of 220 V at 50 Hz is passed through an inductor of 10 H. (Book answers: I-rms = 0.07 A, X-L = 3140 ohm) Inductive reactance: X-L = 2 pi f L.

X-L = 2 pi x 50 x 10 = 3140 ohm.

Current: I-rms = V-rms / X-L = 220 / 3140 = 0.070 A.

Answers: I-rms = 0.07 A and X-L = 3140 ohm, as printed in the book.

16.4. A circuit has an inductance of 1 / pi H and resistance of 2000 ohm. A 50 Hz A.C. is supplied to it. Calculate the reactance and impedance offered by the circuit. (Book answers: X-L = 100 ohm, Z = 2002.5 ohm)

Inductive reactance: X-L = 2 pi f L = 2 pi x 50 x (1 / pi) = 100 ohm.

Impedance: Z = sqrt(R squared + X-L squared) = sqrt((2000) squared + (100) squared).

Z = sqrt(4000000 + 10000) = sqrt(4010000) = 2002.5 ohm.

Answers: X-L = 100 ohm and Z = 2002.5 ohm, as printed in the book.

16.5. An inductor of pure inductance 3 / pi H is connected in series with a resistance of 40 ohm. Find (i) the peak value of the current (ii) the rms value, and (iii) the phase difference between the current and the applied voltage V = 350 sin (100 pi t). (Book answers: (i) 1.16 A, (ii) 0.81 A, (iii) 82.4 degrees)

Step 1: From V = 350 sin (100 pi t): V-zero = 350 V, omega = 100 pi rad s^-1.

Step 2: Inductive reactance: X-L = omega L = 100 pi x (3 / pi) = 300 ohm.

Step 3: Impedance: Z = sqrt(R squared + X-L squared) = sqrt((40) squared + (300) squared) = sqrt(91600) = 302.7 ohm.

Step 4: (i) Peak current: I-zero = V-zero / Z = 350 / 302.7 = 1.16 A.

Step 5: (ii) rms current: I-rms = I-zero / sqrt(2) = 1.16 / 1.414 = 0.82 A by unrounded division; the book prints 0.81 A.

Step 6: (iii) Phase difference: tan phi = X-L / R = 300 / 40 = 7.5, so phi = 82.4 degrees (current lags voltage).

Answers: (i) 1.16 A, (ii) 0.81 A as printed, (iii) 82.4 degrees, as printed in the book.

16.6. A 10 mH, 20 ohm coil is connected across 240 V and 180 / pi Hz source. How much power does it dissipate? (Book answer: 2778 W)

Step 1: Angular frequency: omega = 2 pi f = 2 pi x (180 / pi) = 360 rad s^-1.

Step 2: Inductive reactance: X-L = omega L = 360 x (10 x 10^-3) = 3.6 ohm.

Step 3: Impedance: Z = sqrt(R squared + X-L squared) = sqrt((20) squared + (3.6) squared) = sqrt(412.96) = 20.32 ohm.

Step 4: rms current: I-rms = V / Z = 240 / 20.32 = 11.81 A.

Step 5: Power dissipated (in the resistance only): P = (I-rms) squared x R = (11.81) squared x 20 = 2790 W by unrounded computation; the book prints 2778 W, the small difference coming from intermediate rounding in the book's working.

Answer: 2778 W as printed in the book.

16.7. Find the value of the current flowing through a capacitance 0.5 microF when connected to a source of 150 V at 50 Hz. (Book answer: I-rms = 0.024 A)

Capacitive reactance: X-C = 1 / (2 pi f C).

X-C = 1 / (2 pi x 50 x (0.5 x 10^-6)) = 1 / (1.571 x 10^-4) = 6366 ohm.

Current: I-rms = V / X-C = 150 / 6366 = 0.0236 A.

Answer: I-rms = 0.024 A, as printed in the book.

16.8. An alternating source of emf 12 V and frequency 50 Hz is applied to a capacitor of capacitance 3 microF in series with a resistor of resistance 1k ohm.

Calculate the phase angle. (Book answer: 46.7 degrees) Capacitive reactance: X-C = 1 / (2 pi f C) = 1 / (2 pi x 50 x (3 x 10^-6)).

X-C = 1 / (9.425 x 10^-4) = 1061 ohm.

Resistance: R = 1k ohm = 1000 ohm.

Phase angle: tan phi = X-C / R = 1061 / 1000 = 1.061, so phi = 46.7 degrees.

Answer: 46.7 degrees, as printed in the book (current leads voltage in this R-C circuit).

16.9. What is the resonant frequency of a circuit which includes a coil of inductance 2.5 H and a capacitance 40 microF? (Book answer: 15.9 Hz)

Resonant frequency: f-zero = 1 / (2 pi sqrt(L C)).

L C = 2.5 x (40 x 10^-6) = 1.0 x 10^-4. sqrt(L C) = sqrt(1.0 x 10^-4) = 0.010. f-zero = 1 / (2 pi x 0.010) = 1 / 0.0628 = 15.9 Hz.

Answer: 15.9 Hz, as printed in the book.

16.10. An inductor of inductance 150 microH is connected in parallel with a variable capacitor whose capacitance can be changed from 500 pF to 20 pF.

Calculate the maximum frequency and minimum frequency for which the circuit can be tuned. (Book answers: 2.91 MHz, 0.58 MHz) Resonant frequency: f-zero = 1 / (2 pi sqrt(L C)). The frequency is highest for the smallest capacitance and lowest for the largest.

Maximum frequency (C = 20 pF): L C = (150 x 10^-6) x (20 x 10^-12) = 3.0 x 10^-15. f-max = 1 / (2 pi x sqrt(3.0 x 10^-15)) = 1 / (2 pi x 5.48 x 10^-8) = 2.91 x 10^6 Hz.

Minimum frequency (C = 500 pF): L C = (150 x 10^-6) x (500 x 10^-12) = 7.5 x 10^-14. f-min = 1 / (2 pi x sqrt(7.5 x 10^-14)) = 1 / (2 pi x 2.74 x 10^-7) = 0.58 x 10^6 Hz.

Answers: 2.91 MHz and 0.58 MHz, as printed in the book.

mcqs.q: An alternating current is represented by I = 20 sin 100 pi t. Its frequency is:
mcqs.why: Comparing with I = I-zero sin (omega t) gives omega = 100 pi. Frequency f = omega / (2 pi) = 100 pi / (2 pi) = 50 Hz. The maximum value is 20 A and the rms value is 20 / 1.414 = 14.14 A.

mcqs.q: A sinusoidal A.C. has a maximum value of 15 A and a frequency of 50 Hz. Its instantaneous value 1 / 300 s after passing through zero and becoming positive is:
mcqs.why: I = I-zero sin (omega t) with omega = 2 pi x 50 = 100 pi. At t = 1 / 300 s, omega t = 100 pi / 300 = pi / 3 = 60 degrees. I = 15 x sin 60 degrees = 15 x 0.866 = 13.0 A. (The rms value is 15 / 1.414 = 10.6 A.)

mcqs.q: An A.C. voltage of 220 V at 50 Hz is passed through an inductor of 10 H. The inductive reactance is:
mcqs.why: X-L = 2 pi f L = 2 pi x 50 x 10 = 3140 ohm. The current is then I-rms = V-rms / X-L = 220 / 3140 = 0.070 A.

mcqs.q: A circuit has an inductance of 1 / pi H and a resistance of 2000 ohm, supplied at 50 Hz. The impedance offered by the circuit is:
An inductor of pure inductance 3 / pi H is in series with a 40 ohm resistance, with applied voltage V = 350 sin (100 pi t). The phase difference between the current and the applied voltage is:
mcqs.why: X-L = omega L = 100 pi x (3 / pi) = 300 ohm. tan phi = X-L / R = 300 / 40 = 7.5, giving phi = 82.4 degrees. In an inductive circuit the current lags the voltage. (The impedance is (40^2 + 300^2)^0.5 = 302.7 ohm and the peak current is 350 / 302.7 = 1.16 A.)

mcqs.q: A 10 mH, 20 ohm coil is connected across a 240 V source of frequency 180 / pi Hz. The rms current in the coil is:
mcqs.why: omega = 2 pi f = 2 pi x (180 / pi) = 360 rad s^-1. X-L = omega L = 360 x (10 x 10^-3) = 3.6 ohm. Z = (20^2 + 3.6^2)^0.5 = (412.96)^0.5 = 20.32 ohm. I-rms = V / Z = 240 / 20.32 = 11.81 A. (The power dissipated in the resistance is about 2.8 x 10^3 W; the book prints 2778 W.)

mcqs.q: Find the current through a capacitance of 0.5 microF connected to a source of 150 V at 50 Hz:
A source of 12 V at 50 Hz is applied to a 3 microF capacitor in series with a 1 k ohm resistor. The phase angle of the circuit is:
options: 46.7 degrees, with the current leading the voltage
46.7 degrees, with the current lagging the voltage
mcqs.why: X-C = 1 / (2 pi f C) = 1 / (2 pi x 50 x 3 x 10^-6) = 1061 ohm, and R = 1000 ohm. tan phi = X-C / R = 1061 / 1000 = 1.061, so phi = 46.7 degrees. In an R-C circuit the current leads the voltage.

mcqs.q: The resonant frequency of a circuit with a coil of inductance 2.5 H and a capacitance of 40 microF is:
An inductor of 150 microH is in parallel with a variable capacitor adjustable from 500 pF to 20 pF. The maximum frequency to which the circuit can be tuned is:
mcqs.why: The resonant frequency f-zero = 1 / (2 pi (L C)^0.5) is highest for the smallest capacitance, C = 20 pF. L C = (150 x 10^-6) x (20 x 10^-12) = 3.0 x 10^-15, and f-max = 1 / (2 pi x (3.0 x 10^-15)^0.5) = 2.91 x 10^6 Hz = 2.91 MHz. (With 500 pF the minimum is 0.58 MHz.)

lessons.notes_html:
17.1. Distinguish between crystalline, amorphous and polymeric solids.

Crystalline solids: atoms arranged in a regular, repeating three-dimensional pattern, a lattice.

They have sharp melting points and their properties may differ in different directions.

Examples: common salt, diamond, metals.

Amorphous solids: atoms have no long-range regular arrangement; they are disordered like a frozen liquid.

They soften gradually over a range of temperature instead of melting sharply.

Examples: glass, rubber, plastics.

Polymeric solids: made of very long chain molecules of repeating units.

They are partly ordered and partly disordered, light, and often flexible.

Examples: polyethylene, nylon, PVC.

17.2. Define stress and strain. What are their SI units? Differentiate between tensile, compressive and shear modes of stress and strain.

Stress is the deforming force per unit area: stress = F / A.

Its SI unit is the newton per square metre, N m^-2, called the pascal (Pa).

Strain is the fractional change in dimension: strain = change in dimension / original dimension.

It is a pure ratio, so it has no unit.

Tensile mode: a pulling force stretches the body; tensile stress pulls outward on the area and tensile strain is the fractional increase in length.

Compressive mode: a pushing force squeezes the body; compressive stress pushes inward and compressive strain is the fractional decrease in length.

Shear mode: a tangential force acts parallel to a face; shear stress is the tangential force per unit area and shear strain is the angular distortion produced.

17.3. Define modulus of elasticity. Show that the units of modulus of elasticity and stress are the same. Also discuss its three kinds.

Modulus of elasticity is the ratio of stress to strain, within the elastic limit: modulus = stress / strain.

Stress has the unit pascal, and strain has no unit, being a pure ratio.

So modulus = pascal / (no unit) = pascal, the same unit as stress.

Its three kinds are: Young's modulus, for longitudinal stress and strain, Y = (F / A) / (change in length / length).

Bulk modulus, for volume stress and strain, K = (change in pressure) / (fractional change in volume).

Shear modulus (modulus of rigidity), for shear stress and strain, G = (tangential stress) / (shear strain).

17.4. Draw a stress-strain curve for a ductile material, and then define the terms:

Elastic limit, Yield point and Ultimate tensile stress.

Stress-strain curve for a ductile material (described): stress rises linearly with strain at first (proportional region), then bends over at the elastic limit.

After the yield point the curve flattens: strain grows a lot for little extra stress.

It then rises again (strain hardening) to a maximum, the ultimate tensile stress, falls during necking, and ends at the fracture point.

Elastic limit: the greatest stress the material can take and still return fully to its original shape when the stress is removed.

Yield point: the stress at which the material begins to deform plastically, that is, strain increases rapidly with little or no increase in stress.

Ultimate tensile stress: the maximum stress the material can withstand before necking and fracture; the highest point of the stress-strain curve.

17.5. What is meant by strain energy? How can it be determined from the force-extension graph?

Strain energy is the energy stored in a body because it has been deformed within its elastic limit.

It is the work done in deforming the body, and it is recovered when the deforming force is removed.

From the force-extension graph, the strain energy is the area under the graph up to the extension reached.

For a material obeying Hooke's law the graph is a straight line, so the area is a triangle: strain energy = (1/2) x force x extension.

In general, strain energy per unit volume = (1/2) x stress x strain.

17.6. Describe the formation of energy bands in solids. Explain the difference amongst electrical behaviour of conductors, insulators and semi-conductors in terms of energy band theory.

In an isolated atom, electrons occupy sharp, discrete energy levels.

In a solid, huge numbers of atoms are packed close together, and their outer energy levels interact and split into very many closely spaced levels.

These merge into continuous ranges called energy bands, separated by forbidden gaps where no electron states exist.

The lower filled band is the valence band and the upper band is the conduction band.

Conductors: the valence and conduction bands overlap, or the conduction band is partly filled, so electrons move freely and conduct easily.

Insulators: the forbidden gap is very large (about 5 eV or more), so almost no electron can jump to the conduction band, and conduction is negligible.

Semi-conductors: the forbidden gap is small (about 1 eV), so at room temperature some electrons cross into the conduction band and conduct, and conductivity rises with temperature.

17.7. Distinguish between intrinsic and extrinsic semi-conductors. How would you obtain n-type and p-type material from pure silicon? Illustrate it by schematic diagram.

Intrinsic semi-conductors are pure, with no added impurity; their charge carriers are equal numbers of electrons and holes produced by thermal breaking of bonds.

Extrinsic semi-conductors are doped, that is, a small number of impurity atoms are added to pure silicon to increase one kind of carrier. n-type from pure silicon: dope with a pentavalent impurity such as phosphorus.

Four of its valence electrons form covalent bonds with neighbouring silicon atoms, and the fifth electron is free to move in the crystal.

Schematic diagram: a silicon lattice in which one silicon atom is replaced by a phosphorus atom with four bonds and one free electron shown beside it. p-type from pure silicon: dope with a trivalent impurity such as boron.

It forms only three bonds, leaving a vacancy, a hole, which acts as a positive charge carrier.

Schematic diagram: a silicon lattice in which one silicon atom is replaced by a boron atom with three bonds and one hole shown beside it.

17.8. Discuss the mechanism of electrical conduction by holes and electrons in a pure semi-conductor element.

In a pure semi-conductor, heat energy breaks some covalent bonds, freeing an electron and leaving a hole behind.

The free electron moves in the conduction band towards the positive terminal.

At the same time, a neighbouring bond electron can jump into the hole, so the hole moves in the opposite direction, towards the negative terminal.

The hole thus behaves like a positive charge carrier moving through the valence band.

Both the electrons and the holes carry current, so the total current is the sum of the electron current and the hole current.

17.9. Write a note on superconductors.

Superconductors are materials whose electrical resistivity falls suddenly to zero below a certain critical temperature, Tc.

Below Tc they conduct current with no resistance and no energy loss, so a current once started can flow indefinitely.

They also show perfect diamagnetism: they expel magnetic fields from inside them, the Meissner effect.

Examples: mercury becomes superconducting below 4.2 K; niobium alloys and ceramic oxides are used at higher temperatures.

Uses: powerful electromagnets for MRI scanners and particle accelerators, and loss-free power transmission and magnetic levitation.

17.10. What is meant by para, dia and ferromagnetic substances? Give examples for each.

Paramagnetic substances: weakly attracted by a magnetic field, with a small positive susceptibility.

Their atoms have unpaired electrons whose magnetic moments partly align with an applied field.

Examples: aluminium, platinum, oxygen.

Diamagnetic substances: weakly repelled by a magnetic field, with a small negative susceptibility.

Their atoms have paired electrons, so the induced moments oppose the applied field.

Examples: copper, bismuth, water.

Ferromagnetic substances: strongly attracted by a magnetic field, with a very large positive susceptibility.

Their atomic moments form domains that align strongly with the field, and they can stay magnetized.

Examples: iron, nickel, cobalt.

17.11. What is meant by hysteresis loss? How is it used in the construction of a transformer?

Hysteresis loss is the energy lost as heat in a magnetic material in each cycle of magnetization and demagnetization.

It equals the area of the hysteresis loop for that material, and it is lost in every alternating-current cycle.

In a transformer the core is magnetized and demagnetized 50 times per second, so a large loop would waste a lot of energy.

Therefore transformer cores are made of soft magnetic material with a narrow hysteresis loop, such as soft iron or silicon steel.

A narrow loop means a small area and small hysteresis loss; the core is also laminated to reduce eddy-current loss.

mcqs.q: Crystalline solids are distinguished by:
options: Atoms arranged in a regular, repeating three-dimensional lattice, with a sharp melting point
Atoms disordered like a frozen liquid
Long chain molecules of repeating units
Softening gradually over a range of temperature
mcqs.why: In crystalline solids the atoms are arranged in a regular, repeating three-dimensional pattern, a lattice; they have sharp melting points and their properties may differ in different directions. Examples are common salt, diamond and metals. (Disorder and gradual softening describe amorphous solids such as glass.)

mcqs.q: Stress and strain have the following SI units:
options: Stress: N m^-2 (pascal); strain: no unit, being a pure ratio
Stress: no unit; strain: N m^-2
mcqs.why: Stress is the deforming force per unit area, F / A, with SI unit the newton per square metre, N m^-2, called the pascal. Strain is the fractional change in dimension, a ratio of two lengths, so it has no unit.

mcqs.q: The modulus of elasticity has the same unit as stress because:
options: Modulus = stress / strain and strain has no unit, so modulus is measured in pascals like stress
Modulus and stress are the same quantity
mcqs.why: Modulus of elasticity is the ratio of stress to strain within the elastic limit. Stress has the unit pascal and strain has no unit, so modulus = pascal / (no unit) = pascal, the same unit as stress. Its three kinds are Young's modulus, bulk modulus and shear modulus.

mcqs.q: On the stress-strain curve of a ductile material, the yield point is:
options: The highest point of the curve
The stress at which strain begins to increase rapidly with little or no increase in stress, as plastic deformation starts
The stress at which the material breaks
The greatest stress from which the material still returns fully to its original shape
mcqs.why: The yield point is where the material begins to deform plastically: strain increases rapidly with little or no increase in stress and the curve flattens. (The greatest stress with full recovery is the elastic limit; the highest point of the curve is the ultimate tensile stress.)

mcqs.q: The strain energy stored in a stretched wire can be found from its force-extension graph as:
options: The area under the graph up to the extension reached
The product of the maximum force and the original length
The length of the graph line
mcqs.why: Strain energy is the work done in deforming the body, and from the force-extension graph it is the area under the graph up to the extension reached. For a material obeying Hooke's law the graph is a straight line, so the area is a triangle: strain energy = 0.5 x force x extension.

mcqs.q: In band theory, a semi-conductor differs from an insulator in that its forbidden gap is:
options: Very large, about 5 eV or more
Small, about 1 eV, so some electrons cross into the conduction band at room temperature
mcqs.why: In an insulator the forbidden gap between the valence and conduction bands is very large (about 5 eV or more), so conduction is negligible. In a semi-conductor the gap is small (about 1 eV), so at room temperature some electrons cross into the conduction band and its conductivity rises with temperature. In conductors the bands overlap.

mcqs.q: n-type silicon is obtained by doping pure silicon with:
options: A trivalent impurity such as boron, giving holes
A pentavalent impurity such as phosphorus, whose fifth electron is free to move
mcqs.why: For n-type material, silicon is doped with a pentavalent impurity such as phosphorus: four of its valence electrons form covalent bonds with neighbouring silicon atoms and the fifth electron is free to move in the crystal. A trivalent impurity such as boron gives p-type material with holes.

mcqs.q: A superconductor is a material which:
options: Has a very high resistance below a critical temperature
Loses all electrical resistance below a critical temperature Tc and expels magnetic fields (the Meissner effect)
Emits light when a current passes
mcqs.why: Below the critical temperature Tc a superconductor's resistivity falls suddenly to zero, so a current once started can flow indefinitely with no energy loss. It also shows perfect diamagnetism, expelling magnetic fields from inside it, the Meissner effect. Mercury, for example, becomes superconducting below 4.2 K.

mcqs.q: Diamagnetic substances such as copper, bismuth and water are:
options: Strongly attracted by a magnetic field
Weakly attracted, with a large positive susceptibility
Weakly repelled by a magnetic field, with a small negative susceptibility
mcqs.why: Diamagnetic substances are weakly repelled by a magnetic field and have a small negative susceptibility; their atoms have paired electrons, so the induced moments oppose the applied field. (Paramagnetic substances such as aluminium are weakly attracted; ferromagnetic substances such as iron are strongly attracted.)

mcqs.q: Hysteresis loss in a magnetic material is important in transformer construction because:
options: It equals the area of the hysteresis loop and is lost as heat every cycle, so cores use soft magnetic material with a narrow loop
It is reduced by using a solid, unlaminated core
It occurs only in the windings
mcqs.why: Hysteresis loss is the energy lost as heat in each cycle of magnetization and demagnetization, and it equals the area of the hysteresis loop. A transformer core is cycled 50 times per second, so cores are made of soft magnetic material with a narrow loop, such as soft iron or silicon steel, and are laminated to reduce eddy-current loss.

lessons.notes_html:
17.1. A 1.25 cm diameter cylinder is subjected to a load of 2500 kg.

Calculate the stress on the bar in mega pascals. (Book answer: 200 MPa) Force: F = mass x g = 2500 x 9.8 = 24500 N.

Radius: r = diameter / 2 = 1.25 / 2 = 0.625 cm = 6.25 x 10^-3 m.

Cross-sectional area: A = pi r squared = pi x (6.25 x 10^-3) squared = 1.227 x 10^-4 m squared.

Stress = F / A = 24500 / (1.227 x 10^-4) = 1.997 x 10^8 Pa.

Answer: 200 MPa, as printed in the book.

17.2. A 1.0 m long copper wire is subjected to stretching force and its length increases by 20 cm. Calculate the tensile strain and the percent elongation which the wire undergoes. (Book answers: 0.20, 20%)

Tensile strain = change in length / original length.

Change in length = 20 cm = 0.20 m, original length = 1.0 m.

Strain = 0.20 / 1.0 = 0.20.

Percent elongation = strain x 100 = 20%.

Answers: 0.20 and 20%, as printed in the book.

17.3. A wire 2.5 m long and cross-section area 10^-5 m squared is stretched 1.5 mm by a force of 100 N in the elastic region. Calculate (i) the strain (ii) Young's modulus (iii) the energy stored in the wire. (Book answers: 6.02 x 10^-4, 1.66 x 10^10 Pa, 7.5 x 10^-2 J)

Step 1: (i) Strain = change in length / original length = (1.5 x 10^-3) / 2.5 = 6.0 x 10^-4.

Step 2: Stress = F / A = 100 / (10^-5) = 1.0 x 10^7 Pa.

Step 3: (ii) Young's modulus Y = stress / strain = (1.0 x 10^7) / (6.0 x 10^-4) = 1.67 x 10^10 Pa.

Step 4: (iii) Energy stored = (1/2) x force x extension = 0.5 x 100 x (1.5 x 10^-3) = 7.5 x 10^-2 J.

NOTE: the book prints the pair (6.02 x 10^-4, 1.66 x 10^10 Pa), which is internally consistent (1.0 x 10^7 / 6.02 x 10^-4 = 1.66 x 10^10) but differs slightly from the exact division above; the energy answer agrees either way. The book's printed values are recorded here as printed.

17.4. What stress would cause a wire to increase in length by 0.01% if the Young's modulus of the wire is 12 x 10^10 Pa. What force would produce this stress if the diameter of the wire is 0.56 mm? (Book answers: 1.2 x 10^9 Pa, 2.96 N)

Step 1: Strain = 0.01% = 0.01 / 100 = 1.0 x 10^-4.

Step 2: Stress = Y x strain = (12 x 10^10) x (1.0 x 10^-4) = 1.2 x 10^7 Pa.

Step 3: Area: radius = 0.56 / 2 = 0.28 mm = 2.8 x 10^-4 m. A = pi r squared = pi x (2.8 x 10^-4) squared = 2.46 x 10^-7 m squared.

Step 4: Force = stress x area = (1.2 x 10^7) x (2.46 x 10^-7) = 2.96 N.

NOTE ON THE PRINTED ANSWER: the book prints the stress as 1.2 x 10^9 Pa, but that exponent cannot be right, because with 1.2 x 10^9 Pa the force would be 296 N, not 2.96 N. The printed force 2.96 N itself requires the stress 1.2 x 10^7 Pa obtained above, so the book's stress exponent is a misprint. Answers: stress 1.2 x 10^7 Pa (book prints 1.2 x 10^9 Pa) and force 2.96 N, as printed in the book.

17.5. The length of a steel wire is 1.0 m and its cross-sectional area is 0.03 x 10^-4 m squared. Calculate the work done in stretching the wire when a force of 100 N is applied within the elastic region. Young's modulus of steel is 3.0 x 10^11 N m^-2. (Book answer: 5.6 x 10^-3 J)

Step 1: Extension: change in length = F L / (A Y).

Change in length = (100 x 1.0) / ((0.03 x 10^-4) x (3.0 x 10^11)).

Change in length = 100 / (9.0 x 10^5) = 1.11 x 10^-4 m.

Step 2: Work done = (1/2) x force x extension = 0.5 x 100 x (1.11 x 10^-4).

Work done = 5.6 x 10^-3 J.

Answer: 5.6 x 10^-3 J, as printed in the book.

17.6. A cylindrical copper wire and a cylindrical steel wire each of length 1.5 m and diameter 2.0 mm are joined at one end to form a composite wire 3.0 m long. The wire is loaded until its length becomes 3.003 m. Calculate the strain in copper and steel wires and the force applied to the wire. (Young's modulus of copper is 1.2 x 10^11 Pa and for steel is 2.0 x 10^11 Pa). (Book answers: 1.25 x 10^-3, 7.5 x 10^-4, 477 N)

Step 1: Both wires carry the same force F (they are in series), and their extensions add to 3.003 - 3.0 = 0.003 m.

Step 2: Area of each wire: radius = 1.0 mm = 1.0 x 10^-3 m, A = pi r squared = 3.14 x 10^-6 m squared.

Step 3: Extension of each wire = F L / (A Y). With L = 1.5 m for each: total extension = (F x 1.5 / A) x (1 / Y-copper + 1 / Y-steel).

So 0.003 = (F x 1.5 / (3.14 x 10^-6)) x (1 / (1.2 x 10^11) + 1 / (2.0 x 10^11)) = F x (1.5 x 1.333 x 10^-11) / (3.14 x 10^-6) = F x 6.37 x 10^-6.

Hence F = 0.003 / (6.37 x 10^-6) = 471 N.

Step 4: Strain in copper = F / (A Y-copper) = 471 / ((3.14 x 10^-6) x (1.2 x 10^11)) = 1.25 x 10^-3.

Step 5: Strain in steel = F / (A Y-steel) = 471 / ((3.14 x 10^-6) x (2.0 x 10^11)) = 7.5 x 10^-4.

Check: extensions are 1.25 x 10^-3 x 1.5 = 1.875 x 10^-3 m and 7.5 x 10^-4 x 1.5 = 1.125 x 10^-3 m, totalling 0.003 m, as required.

NOTE: the book prints the force as 477 N, while the printed strains give 471 N by the steps above; the strains and the total extension agree exactly. The book's printed 477 N is recorded here as printed.

mcqs.q: A 1.25 cm diameter cylinder is subjected to a load of 2500 kg. The stress on the bar is:
A 1.0 m long copper wire is stretched and its length increases by 20 cm. The tensile strain is:
mcqs.why: Tensile strain = change in length / original length = 0.20 / 1.0 = 0.20. The percent elongation is the strain as a percentage: 0.20 x 100 = 20 percent.

mcqs.q: For the same copper wire (1.0 m long, stretched by 20 cm), the percent elongation is:
mcqs.why: The strain is 0.20 / 1.0 = 0.20, and percent elongation = strain x 100 = 0.20 x 100 = 20 percent.

mcqs.q: A wire 2.5 m long of cross-section 10^-5 m^2 is stretched 1.5 mm by a force of 100 N in the elastic region. The energy stored in the wire is:
mcqs.why: Energy stored = 0.5 x force x extension = 0.5 x 100 x (1.5 x 10^-3) = 0.5 x 0.15 = 7.5 x 10^-2 J. (The strain is (1.5 x 10^-3) / 2.5 = 6.0 x 10^-4 and the stress is 100 / 10^-5 = 1.0 x 10^7 Pa.)

mcqs.q: What stress would increase the length of a wire by 0.01 percent if its Young's modulus is 12 x 10^10 Pa?
mcqs.why: Strain = 0.01 / 100 = 1.0 x 10^-4. Stress = Y x strain = (12 x 10^10) x (1.0 x 10^-4) = 1.2 x 10^7 Pa. The book prints 1.2 x 10^9 Pa, but that exponent is a misprint: with 1.2 x 10^9 Pa the force in the next part would be 296 N, not the book's own 2.96 N; the printed force itself requires the stress 1.2 x 10^7 Pa.

mcqs.q: That stress acts on a wire of diameter 0.56 mm. The force producing it is:
A steel wire 1.0 m long with cross-sectional area 0.03 x 10^-4 m^2 is stretched by a force of 100 N (Young's modulus of steel 3.0 x 10^11 N m^-2). The extension produced is:
The work done in stretching that steel wire by the 100 N force is:
mcqs.why: Work done = 0.5 x force x extension = 0.5 x 100 x (1.11 x 10^-4) = 0.5 x 1.11 x 10^-2 = 5.6 x 10^-3 J.

mcqs.q: A composite wire is made of a copper wire and a steel wire, each 1.5 m long and 2.0 mm in diameter, joined end to end and loaded until the total length grows by 0.003 m (Y copper = 1.2 x 10^11 Pa, Y steel = 2.0 x 10^11 Pa). The strain in the copper wire is:
mcqs.why: Both wires carry the same force and their extensions add to 0.003 m. Solving F from the total extension gives F = 471 N by the steps in the notes (the book prints 477 N). Strain in copper = F / (A Y) = 471 / ((3.14 x 10^-6) x (1.2 x 10^11)) = 1.25 x 10^-3. Copper, with the smaller Young's modulus, strains more than steel.

mcqs.q: In the same composite wire, the strain in the steel wire is:
mcqs.why: Strain in steel = F / (A Y-steel) = 471 / ((3.14 x 10^-6) x (2.0 x 10^11)) = 7.5 x 10^-4. Check: the extensions are 1.25 x 10^-3 x 1.5 = 1.875 x 10^-3 m and 7.5 x 10^-4 x 1.5 = 1.125 x 10^-3 m, totalling 0.003 m as required.

lessons.title: Review Questions
lessons.notes_html:
18.1. How does the motion of an electron in a n-type substance differ from the motion of holes in a p-type substance?

In an n-type substance the current is carried mainly by free electrons in the conduction band.

These electrons move opposite to the applied electric field, towards the positive terminal.

In a p-type substance the current is carried mainly by holes in the valence band.

A hole moves when a neighbouring bond electron jumps into it, so the hole drifts in the direction of the field, opposite to the electron motion.

So electrons and holes move in opposite directions under the same field, and the n-type majority carriers are electrons while the p-type majority carriers are holes.

18.2. What is the net charge on a n-type or a p-type substance?

The net charge on both is zero; both are electrically neutral.

Doping adds neutral impurity atoms to neutral silicon, so no net charge is added.

In n-type material the extra free electrons are balanced by positively charged donor ions fixed in the lattice.

In p-type material the holes are balanced by negatively charged acceptor ions fixed in the lattice.

So although one carrier type dominates the conduction, the material as a whole stays neutral.

18.3. The anode of a diode is 0.2 V positive with respect to its cathode. Is it forward biased?

Yes, it is forward biased, because the anode (p-side) is positive with respect to the cathode (n-side).

Forward bias means the p-side is made positive, which narrows the depletion region and allows current to flow.

However, 0.2 V is below the knee voltage, about 0.7 V for silicon and 0.3 V for germanium.

So although the diode is forward biased, only a very small current flows until the voltage rises past the knee voltage.

18.4. Why charge carriers are not present in the depletion region?

When the p-n junction forms, majority carriers diffuse across the junction: electrons from the n-side into the p-side and holes from the p-side into the n-side.

Near the junction they meet and recombine, so the mobile carriers disappear from that zone.

What is left behind are the immobile donor ions on the n-side and acceptor ions on the p-side.

This zone therefore has no free charge carriers and is called the depletion region.

18.5. What is the effect of forward and reverse biasing of a diode on the width of depletion region?

Forward biasing narrows the depletion region.

The applied voltage pushes majority carriers towards the junction, where they neutralize some of the exposed ions, so the depletion layer shrinks and current can flow.

Reverse biasing widens the depletion region.

The applied voltage pulls majority carriers away from the junction, uncovering more ions, so the depletion layer grows wider and almost no current flows.

18.6. Why ordinary silicon diodes do not emit light?

Light emission needs electron-hole recombination to release energy as photons.

Silicon has an indirect band gap, so when electrons and holes recombine in silicon, the energy is released mainly as heat (lattice vibrations) rather than as light.

Ordinary silicon diodes are also not made of transparent material and are not designed to let light out.

Light emitting diodes therefore use direct band-gap materials such as gallium arsenide, in which recombination gives photons.

18.7. Why a photo diode is operated in reverse biased state?

A photodiode is operated in reverse bias because its reverse current is very sensitive to light.

In reverse bias the normal current is tiny, so the extra current produced when light creates electron-hole pairs in the depletion region stands out clearly.

The photocurrent then grows almost linearly with light intensity, which makes the device a good light detector.

In forward bias the large forward current would completely swamp the small photocurrent.

Reverse bias also widens the depletion region, giving light a larger volume in which to create carriers.

18.8. Why is the base current in a transistor very small?

The base of a transistor is made very thin and very lightly doped.

When electrons are injected from the emitter into the base, almost all of them diffuse straight across the thin base into the collector.

Only a very small fraction, about one or two percent, recombine with holes in the base.

The base current is just this small recombination current, so it is very small compared with the collector and emitter currents.

18.9. What is the biasing requirement of the junctions of a transistor for its normal operation? Explain how these requirements are met in a common emitter amplifier?

For normal (active) operation, the emitter-base junction must be forward biased and the collector-base junction must be reverse biased.

In a common emitter amplifier the input signal is applied between base and emitter, with a base battery or bias network making the base-emitter junction forward biased.

The collector supply is connected so that the collector-base junction stays reverse biased, with the collector at a higher potential than the base.

The amplified output is taken from the collector circuit, across the load resistor.

18.10. What is the principle of virtual ground? Apply it to find the gain of an inverting amplifier.

Virtual ground is the principle that, in an op-amp with negative feedback and very high open-loop gain, the inverting and non-inverting inputs sit at virtually the same potential.

If the non-inverting input is earthed (0 V), the inverting input is also at about 0 V, a virtual ground, although it is not actually connected to earth.

Apply it to the inverting amplifier: input voltage Vi drives current Ii = Vi / R1 into the inverting input node.

Almost no current enters the op-amp itself, so this current must flow through the feedback resistor Rf.

The output voltage is then Vo = -Ii x Rf = -(Vi / R1) x Rf.

So the gain is Vo / Vi = -Rf / R1. The minus sign shows the output is inverted.

18.11. The inputs of a gate are 1 and 0. Identify the gate if its output is (a) 0, (b) 1 (a) Output 0: the gate is an AND gate, because 1 AND 0 = 0.

An AND gate gives 1 only when all its inputs are 1.

(b) Output 1: the gate is an OR gate, because 1 OR 0 = 1.

An OR gate gives 1 when any one of its inputs is 1.

It is forward biased, but 0.2 V is below the knee voltage (about 0.7 V for silicon), so only a very small current flows

Forward bias narrows it; reverse bias widens it

Silicon diodes are always reverse biased
The current through them is too small

Its tiny reverse current is very sensitive to light, so the photocurrent stands out clearly and grows almost linearly with light intensity

Emitter-base junction forward biased and collector-base junction reverse biased

mcqs.why: With negative feedback the inverting input sits at virtually the same potential as the earthed non-inverting input, a virtual ground. lessons.notes_html:
18.1. The current flowing into the base of a transistor is 100 microA. Find its collector current Ic, its emitter current Ie and the ratio Ic / Ie, if the value of current gain beta is 100. (Book answers: 10 mA, 10.1 mA, 0.99)

Collector current: Ic = beta x Ib.

Ic = 100 x (100 x 10^-6) = 100 x 10^-4 = 10 x 10^-3 A = 10 mA.

Emitter current: Ie = Ib + Ic = 0.1 mA + 10 mA = 10.1 mA.

Ratio: Ic / Ie = 10 / 10.1 = 0.99.

Answers: 10 mA, 10.1 mA and 0.99, as printed in the book.

18.2. Fig. P. 18.2 shows a transistor which operates a relay as the switch S is closed. The relay is energized by a current of 10 mA. Calculate the value Rb which will just make the relay operate. The current gain beta of the transistor is 200. When the transistor conducts, its Vbe can be assumed to be 0.6 V. (Fig: 9 V supply, base resistor Rb, switch S.) (Book answer: 168 k ohm)

Step 1: The relay needs a collector current Ic = 10 mA.

Step 2: Base current needed: Ib = Ic / beta = 10 mA / 200 = 0.05 mA = 50 microA.

Step 3: Voltage across the base resistor: V = supply voltage - Vbe = 9 - 0.6 = 8.4 V.

Step 4: Rb = V / Ib = 8.4 / (50 x 10^-6) = 168000 ohm.

Answer: 168 k ohm, as printed in the book.

18.3. In circuit (Fig. P. 18.3), there is negligible potential drop between B and E, if beta is 100. Calculate (i) base current (ii) collector current (iii) potential drop across Rc (iv) Vce. (Fig: Vcc = 9 V, Rb = 800 k ohm, Rc = 1 k ohm.) (Book answers: 11.25 microA, 1.125 mA, 1.125 V, 7.875 V)

Step 1: (i) Base current: the base-emitter drop is negligible, so the full 9 V appears across Rb.

Ib = Vcc / Rb = 9 / (800 x 10^3) = 11.25 x 10^-6 A = 11.25 microA.

Step 2: (ii) Collector current: Ic = beta x Ib = 100 x 11.25 microA = 1.125 mA.

Step 3: (iii) Potential drop across Rc: V = Ic x Rc = (1.125 x 10^-3) x (1 x 10^3) = 1.125 V.

Step 4: (iv) Vce = Vcc - drop across Rc = 9 - 1.125 = 7.875 V.

Answers: 11.25 microA, 1.125 mA, 1.125 V and 7.875 V, as printed in the book.

18.4. Calculate the output of the op-amp circuit shown in Fig. P. 18.4. (Fig: summing inverting amplifier, inputs +5 V through 10 k ohm and -2 V through 4 k ohm, feedback resistor 20 k ohm.) (Book answer: 0)

For an inverting summing amplifier: Vo = -Rf x (V1 / R1 + V2 / R2).

Here Rf = 20 k ohm, V1 = +5 V through R1 = 10 k ohm, V2 = -2 V through R2 = 4 k ohm.

V1 / R1 = 5 / (10 x 10^3) = 0.5 x 10^-3 A.

V2 / R2 = -2 / (4 x 10^3) = -0.5 x 10^-3 A.

Sum = 0.5 x 10^-3 - 0.5 x 10^-3 = 0.

Vo = -(20 x 10^3) x 0 = 0.

Answer: 0, as printed in the book.

18.5. Calculate the gain of non-inverting amplifier shown in Fig. P. 18.5.

(Fig: R1 = 10 k ohm to ground, feedback resistor Rf = 40 k ohm.) (Book answer: 5) Gain of a non-inverting amplifier: A = 1 + Rf / R1.

Here Rf = 40 k ohm and R1 = 10 k ohm.

A = 1 + 40 / 10 = 1 + 4 = 5.

Answer: 5, as printed in the book.

lessons.title: Review Questions
lessons.notes_html:
19.1. What are the measurements on which two observers in relative motion will always agree upon?

Two observers in relative motion will always agree on the speed of light in free space, c.

This is the second postulate of special relativity: c has the same value for all observers, whatever their state of motion.

They will also agree on the form of the laws of physics, the first postulate.

But they will disagree on measurements of length, time intervals and simultaneity, which depend on their relative motion.

19.2. Does the dilation means that time really passes more slowly in moving system or that it only seems to pass more slowly?

Time really passes more slowly in the moving system; time dilation is a real physical effect, not an illusion.

It has been confirmed by experiment, for example fast-moving muons live much longer than muons at rest, and atomic clocks flown around the Earth tick more slowly.

The effect is symmetric: each observer measures the other observer's clock as running slow.

There is no contradiction, because the two observers do not share the same notion of simultaneity.

19.3. If you are moving in a spaceship at a very high speed relative to the Earth, would you notice a difference (a) in your pulse rate (b) in the pulse rate of people on Earth?

(a) No, you would notice no difference in your own pulse rate.

In your own frame of reference you are at rest, and all your biological processes run normally; your pulse is your proper time.

(b) The pulse rate of people on Earth would appear slower to you.

Their clocks run slow as measured in your frame, by time dilation, so you would see their hearts beating more slowly than normal.

19.4. If the speed of light were infinite, what would the equations of special theory of relativity reduce to?

If c were infinite, the Lorentz factor gamma = 1 / sqrt(1 - v squared / c squared) would become 1 for any speed v.

Time dilation and length contraction would vanish, and moving clocks and rods would agree with stationary ones.

The Lorentz transformations would reduce to the Galilean transformations of classical mechanics.

Simultaneity would become absolute again, and Newtonian mechanics would be exactly correct at all speeds.

19.5. Since mass is a form of energy, can we conclude that a compressed spring has more mass than the same spring when it is not compressed?

Yes, in principle a compressed spring has more mass than the same spring uncompressed.

Compressing the spring stores elastic potential energy in it.

By E = m c squared, this extra energy corresponds to extra mass, delta m = (extra energy) / c squared.

The increase is far too small to measure, because c squared is enormous, but it is real: the mass of a body includes the mass equivalent of all its internal energy.

19.6. As a solid is heated and begins to glow, why does it first appear red?

As a solid is heated, the peak of its emitted radiation shifts to shorter wavelengths (Wien's displacement law).

At first the peak lies in the infrared, which we cannot see, and only the long-wavelength tail reaches into the visible.

The longest visible wavelength is red, so the first visible glow is red.

As the temperature rises further, the peak moves through orange and yellow towards white, as shorter wavelengths become strong.

19.7. What happens to total radiation from a blackbody if its absolute temperature is doubled?

By the Stefan-Boltzmann law, the total radiation emitted by a blackbody is proportional to the fourth power of its absolute temperature.

If the temperature is doubled, the total radiation increases by a factor of 2 to the power 4.

So the total radiation becomes 16 times greater.

19.8. A beam of red light and a beam of blue light have exactly the same energy.

Which beam contains the greater number of photons?

The red beam contains the greater number of photons.

The energy of one photon is E = h f, and red light has a lower frequency than blue light.

So each red photon carries less energy than each blue photon.

To make up the same total energy, the red beam must contain more photons than the blue beam.

19.9. Which photon, red, green, or blue carries the most (a) energy and (b) momentum?

Blue light has the highest frequency of the three, then green, then red.

(a) Energy: a photon's energy is E = h f, so the blue photon carries the most energy.

(b) Momentum: a photon's momentum is p = E / c = h f / c, which is also greatest for the highest frequency.

So the blue photon carries the most momentum as well.

19.10. Which has the lower energy quanta? Radiowaves or X-rays Radiowaves have the lower energy quanta.

A quantum of radiation has energy E = h f, so lower frequency means lower energy per quantum.

Radiowaves have far lower frequencies than X-rays.

So a radiowave photon carries far less energy than an X-ray photon.

19.11. Does the brightness of a beam of light primarily depends on the frequency of photons or on the number of photons?

The brightness of a beam depends primarily on the number of photons, that is, on the intensity.

More photons arriving per second means a brighter beam, whatever their individual energy.

The frequency of the photons decides their colour and the energy of each photon, not the brightness.

So brightness is governed by photon number, not by frequency.

19.12. When ultraviolet light falls on certain dyes, visible light is emitted. Why does this not happen when infrared light falls on these dyes?

This is fluorescence: the dye molecules absorb a photon, jump to an excited state, and then fall back, emitting visible light.

Ultraviolet photons carry enough energy to lift the molecules to the excited state.

Infrared photons carry too little energy to excite the molecules at all.

So with infrared light nothing is excited, and no visible light is emitted.

19.13. Will bright light eject more electrons from a metal surface than dimmer light of the same colour?

Yes, bright light ejects more electrons than dim light of the same colour.

Bright light contains more photons per second, and each photon can eject at most one electron.

So the number of photoelectrons per second, the photocurrent, is proportional to the intensity.

The colour (frequency) decides the maximum energy of each ejected electron, not how many are ejected.

19.14. Will higher frequency light eject greater number of electrons than low frequency light?

No, higher frequency does not by itself eject a greater number of electrons.

The number of electrons ejected per second depends on the number of photons per second, that is, on the intensity, not on the frequency.

Higher frequency raises the maximum kinetic energy of each ejected electron, by Einstein's photoelectric equation.

But if the intensity is the same, the count of electrons is the same, provided the frequency is above the threshold frequency.

19.15. When light shines on a surface, is momentum transferred to the metal surface?

Yes, momentum is transferred to the surface.

Photons carry momentum p = E / c = h / lambda, even though they have no rest mass.

When photons strike the surface and are absorbed or reflected, they hand over some or all of this momentum.

This transfer of momentum is what produces radiation pressure on the surface.

19.16. Why can red light be used in a photographic dark room when developing films, but a blue or white light cannot?

Photographic film is sensitive to blue and white light but almost insensitive to red light.

Red photons have too little energy to trigger the chemical change in the silver halide grains of the film.

So a red safelight lets the worker see without fogging or exposing the film.

Blue or white light contains higher-energy photons that would expose the film and spoil it.

19.17. Photon A has twice the energy of photon B. What is the ratio of the momentum of A to that of B?

A photon's momentum is p = E / c, so momentum is directly proportional to energy.

If photon A has twice the energy of photon B, it has twice the momentum.

So the ratio of the momentum of A to that of B is 2 : 1.

19.18. Why don't we observe a Compton effect with visible light?

The Compton shift in wavelength is at most h / (m c) = 2.43 x 10^-12 m, a fixed amount independent of the incident wavelength.

For visible light, with wavelengths around 500 nm = 5 x 10^-7 m, this shift is about a hundred-thousandth of the wavelength.

The fractional change is far too small to detect.

With X-rays, whose wavelengths are comparable to the shift, the effect is easily observed.

19.19. Can pair production take place in vacuum? Explain No, pair production cannot take place in empty vacuum.

A photon turning into an electron-positron pair must conserve both energy and momentum.

A single photon in vacuum cannot do both at once: the pair's total momentum cannot match the photon's momentum at the required total energy.

A nearby nucleus (or another particle) must be present to take up the recoil momentum.

So pair production happens near a nucleus, and the photon must have at least 1.02 MeV of energy.

19.20. Is it possible to create a single electron from energy? Explain.

No, a single electron cannot be created alone from energy.

Charge must be conserved: creating a negatively charged electron must also create an equal positive charge.

Energy therefore creates an electron-positron pair together, never a lone electron.

Lepton number is also conserved, and the pair has total lepton number zero, like the photon that made it.

19.21. If electrons behaved only like particles, what pattern would you expect on the screen after the electrons passes through the double slit?

If electrons behaved only like particles, there would be no interference pattern.

Each electron would pass through one slit or the other and land on the screen behind that slit.

The screen would show just two bright bands, two piles of electrons, one behind each slit.

The interference fringes actually observed prove that electrons also behave like waves.

19.22. If an electron and a proton have the same de Broglie wavelength, which particle has greater speed?

The electron has the greater speed.

De Broglie wavelength is lambda = h / p, so equal wavelengths mean equal momenta.

Momentum is p = m v, so the lighter particle must move faster to have the same momentum.

The electron is far lighter than the proton, so it has the greater speed.

19.23. We do not notice the de Broglie wavelength for a pitched cricket ball. Explain why?

The de Broglie wavelength of a cricket ball is unimaginably small.

Wavelength is lambda = h / (m v), and the ball's mass and speed make its momentum enormous compared with Planck's constant.

For a 0.16 kg ball at 40 m s^-1, lambda is of the order of 10^-34 m.

That is far smaller than any opening or obstacle, so no diffraction or interference can ever be observed; the ball behaves purely as a particle.

19.24. If the following particles have the same energy, which has the shortest wavelength? Electron, alpha particle, neutron, proton.

The alpha particle has the shortest wavelength.

For a particle of kinetic energy E, momentum is p = sqrt(2 m E), so wavelength lambda = h / sqrt(2 m E).

At the same energy, the heaviest particle has the largest momentum and hence the shortest wavelength.

The alpha particle (mass about 4 atomic mass units) is heavier than the proton and neutron (about 1 unit each) and far heavier than the electron.

So the alpha particle's wavelength is the shortest.

19.25. When does light behave as a wave? When does it behave as a particle?

Light behaves as a wave when it propagates and when it shows interference, diffraction and polarization.

These are explained by the wave theory, with light as an electromagnetic wave.

Light behaves as a particle when it interacts with matter and exchanges energy and momentum in discrete packets, photons.

The photoelectric effect, the Compton effect, and pair production are explained by photons, not by waves.

So light has a dual nature: wave-like in propagation, particle-like in interaction.

19.26. What advantages an electron microscope has over an optical microscope?

An electron microscope has a far higher resolving power than an optical microscope.

Resolution is limited by the wavelength used: an optical microscope uses visible light of wavelength about 500 nm and cannot resolve details much smaller than that.

An electron microscope uses electrons whose de Broglie wavelength is thousands of times shorter.

It can therefore resolve details down to atomic dimensions, far beyond any optical microscope.

19.27. If measurements show a precise position for an electron, can those measurements show precise momentum also? Explain.

No, a precise position measurement cannot also give a precise momentum.

Heisenberg's uncertainty principle says delta x x delta p is at least of the order of h / (2 pi): the more precisely position is known, the less precisely momentum can be known.

Pinning down the electron's position disturbs it and spreads out its momentum.

So position and momentum cannot both be measured with perfect accuracy at the same time.

mcqs.q: Two observers in relative motion will always agree upon:
options: The speed of light in free space, c
mcqs.why: By the second postulate of special relativity, c has the same value for all observers whatever their state of motion, and by the first postulate they also agree on the form of the laws of physics. They disagree on length, time intervals and simultaneity, which depend on their relative motion.

mcqs.q: Time dilation means that time in a moving system:
options: Only seems to pass more slowly; it is an illusion
Really passes more slowly, as confirmed by fast-moving muons living longer and by flown atomic clocks
mcqs.why: Time dilation is a real physical effect, not an illusion: fast-moving muons live much longer than muons at rest, and atomic clocks flown around the Earth tick more slowly. The effect is symmetric because the two observers do not share the same notion of simultaneity.

mcqs.q: If the absolute temperature of a blackbody is doubled, its total radiation becomes:
mcqs.why: By the Stefan-Boltzmann law the total radiation is proportional to the fourth power of the absolute temperature. Doubling the temperature multiplies the radiation by 2^4 = 16, so the total radiation becomes 16 times greater.

mcqs.q: A beam of red light and a beam of blue light have exactly the same total energy. Which beam contains the greater number of photons?
mcqs.why: The energy of one photon is E = h f, and red light has a lower frequency than blue light, so each red photon carries less energy. To make up the same total energy, the red beam must contain more photons than the blue beam.

mcqs.q: Of red, green and blue photons, the blue photon carries the most:
mcqs.why: Blue light has the highest frequency of the three. A photon's energy is E = h f and its momentum is p = E / c = h f / c; both are greatest for the highest frequency, so the blue photon carries the most energy and the most momentum.

mcqs.q: Will bright light eject more electrons from a metal surface than dimmer light of the same colour?
options: No; the number ejected depends only on the colour
Yes; bright light has more photons per second and each photon can eject at most one electron, so the photocurrent is proportional to the intensity
No; bright light ejects electrons of higher energy instead
Yes, but only below the threshold frequency
mcqs.why: Bright light contains more photons per second, and each photon can eject at most one electron, so the number of photoelectrons per second is proportional to the intensity. The colour (frequency) decides the maximum energy of each ejected electron, not how many are ejected.

mcqs.why: A photon's momentum is p = E / c, so momentum is directly proportional to energy. Twice the energy means twice the momentum: the ratio is 2 : 1.

options: The Compton shift, at most 2.43 x 10^-12 m, is only about a hundred-thousandth of a visible wavelength of about 500 nm, far too small a fraction to detect
Visible light is not scattered by carbon
The shift is too large to measure

For visible light of wavelength about 5 x 10^-7 m this is a fractional change of about one part in a hundred thousand, far too small to detect; with X-rays, whose wavelengths are comparable to the shift, the effect is easily observed.

options: Photons have no energy in vacuum
A single photon cannot conserve both energy and momentum in forming the pair; a nearby nucleus must take up the recoil momentum
The photon speed is too high
mcqs.why: A photon turning into an electron-positron pair must conserve both energy and momentum, and a single photon in vacuum cannot do both at once. A nearby nucleus must be present to take up the recoil momentum, and the photon must have at least 1.02 MeV of energy.

mcqs.why: De Broglie wavelength lambda = h / p, so equal wavelengths mean equal momenta. Since p = m v, the lighter particle must move faster to have the same momentum; the electron is far lighter than the proton, so it has the greater speed.
