19.1. A particle called the pion lives on the average only about 2.6 x 10^-8 s when at rest in the laboratory. It then changes to another form. How long would such a particle live when shooting through the space at 0.95 c? (Book answer: 8.3 x 10^-8 s)

Time dilation: moving lifetime = gamma x rest lifetime, with gamma = 1 / sqrt(1 - v squared / c squared).

Here v / c = 0.95, so gamma = 1 / sqrt(1 - 0.9025) = 1 / sqrt(0.0975) = 1 / 0.3122 = 3.20.

Moving lifetime = 3.20 x (2.6 x 10^-8) = 8.3 x 10^-8 s.

Answer: 8.3 x 10^-8 s, as printed in the book.

19.2. What is the mass of a 70 kg man in a space rocket travelling at 0.8 c from us as measured from Earth? (Book answer: 116.7 kg)

Relativistic mass: m = m-zero / sqrt(1 - v squared / c squared).

Here v / c = 0.8, so sqrt(1 - 0.64) = sqrt(0.36) = 0.60. m = 70 / 0.60 = 116.7 kg.

Answer: 116.7 kg, as printed in the book.

19.3. Find the energy of photon in (b) Radiowave of wavelength 100 m (c) Green light of wavelength 550 nm (d) X-ray with wavelength 0.2 nm (Book answers: (a) 1.24 x 10^-6 eV (b) 2.25 eV (c) 6200 eV)

Photon energy: E = h c / lambda. With h c = 1240 eV nm, E (in eV) = 1240 / lambda (in nm).

Radiowave: the book's answer 1.24 x 10^-6 eV requires lambda = 1 m = 10^9 nm:

E = 1240 / 10^9 = 1.24 x 10^-6 eV. (If the wavelength were literally 100 m, E would be 1.24 x 10^-8 eV; the stem's '100 m' is most plausibly the printed '10^0 m' = 1 m.)

Green light: lambda = 550 nm, E = 1240 / 550 = 2.25 eV.

X-ray: lambda = 0.2 nm, E = 1240 / 0.2 = 6200 eV.

Answers: 1.24 x 10^-6 eV, 2.25 eV and 6200 eV, as printed in the book (note the radiowave part above).

19.4. Yellow light of 577 nm wavelength is incident on a cesium surface.

The stopping voltage is found to be 0.25 V. Find (a) the Maximum K.E. of the photoelectrons (b) the work function of cesium (Book answers: (a) 4 x 10^-20 J (b) 1.91 eV)

Step 1: (a) Maximum kinetic energy = e x stopping voltage = 0.25 eV.

In joules: 0.25 x (1.60 x 10^-19) = 4.0 x 10^-20 J.

Step 2: Photon energy: E = h c / lambda = 1240 / 577 = 2.15 eV.

Step 3: (b) Work function: phi = E - K.E.-max = 2.15 - 0.25 = 1.90 eV by this rounding; the book prints 1.91 eV.

Answers: (a) 4 x 10^-20 J and (b) 1.91 eV, as printed in the book.

19.5. X-rays of wavelength 22 pm are scattered from a carbon target. The scattered radiation being viewed at 85 degrees to the incident beam. What is Compton shift? (Book answer: 2.2 x 10^-12 m)

Compton shift: change in lambda = (h / (m c)) x (1 - cos theta), with h / (m c) = 2.43 x 10^-12 m.

Here theta = 85 degrees, cos 85 degrees = 0.0872.

Change in lambda = (2.43 x 10^-12) x (1 - 0.0872) = (2.43 x 10^-12) x 0.9128.

Change in lambda = 2.2 x 10^-12 m.

Answer: 2.2 x 10^-12 m, as printed in the book.

19.6. A 90 keV X-ray photon is fired at a carbon target and Compton scattering occurs. Find the wavelength of the incident photon and the wavelength of the scattered photon for scattering angle of (a) 30 degrees (b) 60 degrees (Book answers: 13.8 pm (a) 14.1 pm (b) 15 pm)

Step 1: Incident wavelength: lambda = h c / E = 1240 eV nm / 90000 eV = 0.0138 nm = 13.8 pm.

Step 2: Compton shift: change in lambda = (2.43 pm) x (1 - cos theta).

Step 3: (a) theta = 30 degrees: change = 2.43 x (1 - 0.866) = 2.43 x 0.134 = 0.33 pm.

Scattered wavelength = 13.8 + 0.33 = 14.1 pm.

Step 4: (b) theta = 60 degrees: change = 2.43 x (1 - 0.500) = 2.43 x 0.500 = 1.22 pm.

Scattered wavelength = 13.8 + 1.22 = 15.0 pm.

Answers: 13.8 pm, (a) 14.1 pm and (b) 15 pm, as printed in the book.

19.7. What is the maximum wavelength of the two photons produced when a positron annihilates an electron? The rest mass energy of each is 0.51 MeV.

(Book answer: 2.44 x 10^-12 m) In annihilation the total rest energy, 2 x 0.51 = 1.02 MeV, appears as two photons.

The longest wavelength corresponds to the smallest photon energy, when the energy is shared equally: each photon gets 0.51 MeV.

Wavelength: lambda = h c / E = 1240 MeV fm / 0.51 MeV = 2431 fm.

Answer: 2.44 x 10^-12 m, as printed in the book.

19.8. Calculate the wavelength of (a) a 140 g ball moving at 40 m s^-1 (b) a proton moving at the same speed (c) an electron moving at the same speed (Book answers: (a) 1.18 x 10^-34 m (b) 9.92 nm (c) 1.82 x 10^-5 m)

De Broglie wavelength: lambda = h / (m v), with h = 6.63 x 10^-34 J s and v = 40 m s^-1.

(a) Ball: m = 140 g = 0.14 kg. lambda = (6.63 x 10^-34) / (0.14 x 40) = (6.63 x 10^-34) / 5.6 = 1.18 x 10^-34 m.

(b) Proton: m = 1.67 x 10^-27 kg. lambda = (6.63 x 10^-34) / ((1.67 x 10^-27) x 40) = (6.63 x 10^-34) / (6.68 x 10^-26) = 9.92 x 10^-9 m = 9.92 nm.

(c) Electron: m = 9.11 x 10^-31 kg. lambda = (6.63 x 10^-34) / ((9.11 x 10^-31) x 40) = (6.63 x 10^-34) / (3.64 x 10^-29) = 1.82 x 10^-5 m.

Answers: (a) 1.18 x 10^-34 m, (b) 9.92 nm and (c) 1.82 x 10^-5 m, as printed in the book.

19.9. What is the de Broglie wavelength of an electron whose kinetic energy is 120 eV? (Book answer: 1.12 x 10^-10 m)

Momentum from kinetic energy: p = sqrt(2 m K).

K = 120 eV = 120 x (1.60 x 10^-19) = 1.92 x 10^-17 J. m = 9.11 x 10^-31 kg. p = sqrt(2 x (9.11 x 10^-31) x (1.92 x 10^-17)) = sqrt(3.50 x 10^-47) = 5.92 x 10^-24 kg m s^-1.

Wavelength: lambda = h / p = (6.63 x 10^-34) / (5.92 x 10^-24) = 1.12 x 10^-10 m.

Answer: 1.12 x 10^-10 m, as printed in the book.

19.10. An electron is placed in a box about the size of an atom that is about 1.0 x 10^-10 m. What is the velocity of the electron? (Book answer: 7.29 x 10^6 m s^-1)

Uncertainty principle (book's form): delta x x delta p is of the order of h.

With delta x = 1.0 x 10^-10 m: delta p = h / delta x = (6.63 x 10^-34) / (1.0 x 10^-10) = 6.63 x 10^-24 kg m s^-1.

Velocity: v = delta p / m = (6.63 x 10^-24) / (9.11 x 10^-31) = 7.28 x 10^6 m s^-1.

Answer: 7.29 x 10^6 m s^-1, as printed in the book.

What is the mass of a 70 kg man in a rocket travelling at 0.8 c, as measured from Earth?

lessons.notes_html:
20.1. Bohr's theory of hydrogen atom is based upon several assumptions. Do any of these assumptions contradict classical physics?

Yes, two of Bohr's assumptions contradict classical physics.

First, Bohr assumed that an electron in a stationary orbit does not radiate energy, although classical electrodynamics says an accelerating (circularly moving) charge must radiate and spiral into the nucleus.

Second, he assumed that the electron's angular momentum is quantized, L = n h / (2 pi), whereas classical physics allows angular momentum to take any value.

Bohr's theory was therefore a hybrid: classical mechanics for the orbits, plus quantum rules imposed on them.

20.2. What is meant by a line spectrum? Explain, how line spectrum can be used for the identification of elements?

A line spectrum is a spectrum consisting of separate bright lines at definite wavelengths, with darkness in between, instead of a continuous rainbow.

It is produced when excited atoms emit light: each line corresponds to a transition between two energy levels of the atom.

Every element has its own unique set of energy levels, so its line pattern is unique, like a fingerprint.

By matching an unknown sample's lines with known spectra, the elements present in the sample can be identified.

20.3. Can the electron in the ground state of hydrogen absorb a photon of energy 13.6 eV and greater than 13.6 eV?

Yes, it can absorb both.

The ground-state energy of hydrogen is -13.6 eV, so a photon of exactly 13.6 eV gives the electron just enough energy to escape the atom: the atom is ionized.

A photon of energy greater than 13.6 eV is also absorbed, and the extra energy beyond 13.6 eV becomes the kinetic energy of the freed electron.

A photon of less than 13.6 eV, not equal to any level difference, cannot be absorbed at all.

20.4. How can the spectrum of hydrogen contain so many lines when hydrogen contains one electron?

Each hydrogen atom has only one electron, but a glowing sample contains a huge number of atoms.

At any moment, different atoms have their electrons in different excited states.

Each atom's electron can drop through many possible pairs of levels, and each possible transition gives one spectral line.

The spectrum we see is the combined light of all the atoms, so it contains lines for every allowed transition, even though each atom contributes only one line at a time.

20.5. Is energy conserved when an atom emits a photon of light?

Yes, energy is fully conserved when an atom emits a photon.

The photon's energy is exactly the difference between the atom's higher and lower energy levels: h f = E-higher - E-lower.

The atom's internal energy falls by exactly the amount the photon carries away.

Total energy, atom plus photon, stays the same; the tiny recoil energy of the atom is negligible.

20.6. Explain why a glowing gas gives only certain wavelengths of light and why that gas is capable of absorbing the same wavelengths? Give a reason why it is transparent to other wavelengths?

A glowing gas emits light when its excited electrons fall to lower energy levels.

Each fall releases a photon whose energy equals the difference of the two levels, so only the wavelengths matching level differences appear: the emission spectrum is a set of lines.

The same gas absorbs light when a ground-state electron jumps up by absorbing a photon of exactly a level-difference energy.

So it absorbs the same wavelengths it emits.

Other wavelengths match no level difference, so no electron can absorb them; they pass straight through, and the gas is transparent to them.

20.7. What do we mean when we say that the atom is excited?

An atom is excited when one of its electrons has been raised from the ground state to a higher energy level.

This happens when the atom absorbs energy, for example from a photon or a collision.

The excited state is unstable, and after a short time the electron falls back, emitting the extra energy as a photon.

20.8. Can X-rays be reflected, refracted, diffracted and polarized just like any other waves? Explain.

Yes, X-rays show all these wave properties, because they are electromagnetic waves like visible light.

They can be reflected and refracted, though the effects are small because their wavelengths are so short.

They are diffracted by crystal lattices, whose atomic spacings are comparable to X-ray wavelengths; this is the basis of X-ray crystallography.

They can also be polarized, for example by scattering, just like visible light.

20.9. What are the advantages of lasers over ordinary light?

Lasers are monochromatic: they emit light of essentially a single wavelength, unlike ordinary light which mixes many wavelengths.

Lasers are coherent: all their waves are in phase with each other, so they interfere constructively and stay in step.

Lasers are highly directional: the beam spreads very little and stays narrow over long distances.

Lasers are very intense: a large power can be concentrated into a tiny area, which is why they can cut, drill and carry signals.

20.10. Explain why laser action could not occur without population inversion between atomic levels?

Laser action needs stimulated emission to outnumber absorption.

Normally most atoms sit in the lower level, so an incoming photon is more likely to be absorbed by a lower-level atom than to stimulate an upper-level atom.

Population inversion reverses this: more atoms are in the upper level than in the lower level.

Then stimulated emission dominates, each photon produces two identical photons, and the beam is amplified.

Without inversion there is net absorption, not amplification, and no laser action.

mcqs.q: Which of Bohr's assumptions contradict classical physics?
options: That electrons move in circular orbits
That an electron in a stationary orbit does not radiate, and that its angular momentum is quantized as L = n h / (2 pi)
That the nucleus is positively charged
That spectral lines are emitted by atoms
mcqs.why: Classical electrodynamics says an accelerating (circularly moving) charge must radiate and spiral into the nucleus, but Bohr assumed an electron in a stationary orbit does not radiate. He also assumed the angular momentum is quantized, L = n h / (2 pi), whereas classical physics allows it to take any value.

mcqs.q: A line spectrum can be used to identify elements because:
options: All elements give the same lines
Each element has its own unique set of energy levels, so its line pattern is unique, like a fingerprint
The lines show the mass of the atoms
mcqs.why: A line spectrum consists of separate bright lines at definite wavelengths, each line corresponding to a transition between two energy levels of the atom. Every element has its own unique set of levels, so by matching an unknown sample's lines with known spectra, the elements present can be identified.

mcqs.q: Can the electron in the ground state of hydrogen absorb a photon of energy 13.6 eV, or of energy greater than 13.6 eV?
options: It can absorb 13.6 eV but nothing greater
It can absorb both: 13.6 eV just ionizes the atom, and any extra energy beyond 13.6 eV becomes kinetic energy of the freed electron
It can absorb any photon energy, including less than 13.6 eV
mcqs.why: The ground-state energy of hydrogen is -13.6 eV. A photon of exactly 13.6 eV gives the electron just enough energy to escape, ionizing the atom; a more energetic photon is also absorbed, the excess becoming the kinetic energy of the freed electron. A photon of less than 13.6 eV that matches no level difference cannot be absorbed at all.

mcqs.q: How can the spectrum of hydrogen contain so many lines when each hydrogen atom has only one electron?
options: Each electron emits all the lines at once
A glowing sample contains a huge number of atoms whose electrons are in different excited states, and every allowed transition in some atom contributes a line
The electron splits into several electrons
The lines come from the nucleus
mcqs.why: At any moment, different atoms in the sample have their electrons in different excited states, and each atom's electron can drop through many possible pairs of levels. The observed spectrum is the combined light of all the atoms, so it contains lines for every allowed transition, even though each atom contributes only one line at a time.

mcqs.q: When an atom emits a photon, is energy conserved?
options: No; the photon's energy is created from nothing
Yes; the photon's energy is exactly the difference between the atom's higher and lower levels, h f = E-higher - E-lower
Only if the atom is hydrogen
Energy is conserved only in absorption
mcqs.why: The atom's internal energy falls by exactly the amount the photon carries away: h f = E-higher - E-lower. Total energy, atom plus photon, stays the same; the tiny recoil energy of the atom is negligible.

mcqs.q: Why is a glowing gas transparent to wavelengths other than the ones it emits and absorbs?
options: Those wavelengths are reflected by the gas
They match no energy-level difference, so no electron can absorb them and they pass straight through
The gas is too thin for them
They are absorbed by the container instead
mcqs.why: Emission and absorption both require photons whose energy equals the difference of two energy levels of the atom, so the gas absorbs the same wavelengths it emits. Other wavelengths match no level difference, no electron can absorb them, and they pass straight through.

mcqs.q: An atom is said to be excited when:
options: One of its electrons has been raised from the ground state to a higher energy level
mcqs.why: An atom is excited when one of its electrons has absorbed energy, for example from a photon or a collision, and been raised to a higher energy level. The excited state is unstable, and after a short time the electron falls back, emitting the extra energy as a photon.

mcqs.q: X-rays are diffracted by crystal lattices because:
options: The atomic spacings in crystals are comparable to X-ray wavelengths, which is the basis of X-ray crystallography
mcqs.why: X-rays are electromagnetic waves like visible light and can be reflected, refracted, diffracted and polarized. Crystal lattices diffract them because the spacings between the atoms are comparable to X-ray wavelengths; this is the basis of X-ray crystallography.

mcqs.q: Which of the following is NOT an advantage of laser light over ordinary light listed in the notes?
options: It contains many wavelengths mixed together
mcqs.why: Lasers are monochromatic (essentially a single wavelength, unlike ordinary light which mixes many wavelengths), coherent (all waves in phase), highly directional (the beam spreads very little) and very intense. Containing many wavelengths describes ordinary light, not laser light.

mcqs.q: Laser action could not occur without population inversion because:
options: Atoms would emit no photons at all
Without more atoms in the upper level than the lower, an incoming photon is more likely to be absorbed than to stimulate emission, giving net absorption instead of amplification
The levels would change their energies
mcqs.why: Laser action needs stimulated emission to outnumber absorption. Normally most atoms sit in the lower level, so photons are absorbed. Population inversion puts more atoms in the upper level, so each photon produces two identical photons and the beam is amplified.

20.1. A hydrogen atoms is in its ground state (n = 1). Using Bohr's theory, calculate (a) the radius of the orbit, (b) the linear momentum of the electron, (c) the angular momentum of the electron (d) the kinetic energy (e) the potential energy, and (f) the total energy. (Book answers: (a) 0.529 x 10^-10 m (b) 1.99 x 10^-24 kg m s^-1 (c) 1.05 x 10^-34 kg m squared s^-1 (d) 13.6 eV (e) -27.2 eV (f) -13.6 eV)

Step 1: (a) Bohr radius for n = 1: r1 = 0.529 x 10^-10 m.

Step 2: (b) Speed in the ground state: v = 2.18 x 10^6 m s^-1. Linear momentum p = m v = (9.11 x 10^-31) x (2.18 x 10^6). p = 1.99 x 10^-24 kg m s^-1.

Step 3: (c) Angular momentum: L = n h / (2 pi) = (6.63 x 10^-34) / (2 pi) = 1.05 x 10^-34 kg m squared s^-1.

Step 4: (d) Kinetic energy = +13.6 eV (the electron's motion energy in the ground state).

Step 5: (e) Potential energy = -2 x kinetic energy = -27.2 eV.

Step 6: (f) Total energy = kinetic + potential = 13.6 - 27.2 = -13.6 eV.

Answers: (a) 0.529 x 10^-10 m, (b) 1.99 x 10^-24 kg m s^-1, (c) 1.05 x 10^-34 kg m squared s^-1, (d) 13.6 eV, (e) -27.2 eV and (f) -13.6 eV, as printed in the book.

20.2. What are the energies in eV of quanta of wavelength? lambda = 400, 500 and 700 nm. (Book answers: 3.10 eV, 2.49 eV, 1.77 eV)

Photon energy: E = h c / lambda, with h c = 1240 eV nm.

For 400 nm: E = 1240 / 400 = 3.10 eV.

For 500 nm: E = 1240 / 500 = 2.48 eV by this value of h c; the book prints 2.49 eV.

For 700 nm: E = 1240 / 700 = 1.77 eV.

Answers: 3.10 eV, 2.49 eV and 1.77 eV, as printed in the book.

20.3. An electron jumps from a level Ei = -3.5 x 10^-19 J to Ef = -1.20 x 10^-18 J. What is the wavelength of the emitted light? (Book answer: 234 nm)

The electron falls from the higher level Ei = -3.5 x 10^-19 J to the lower level Ef = -1.20 x 10^-18 J.

Photon energy = Ei - Ef = (-3.5 x 10^-19) - (-1.20 x 10^-18) = 8.5 x 10^-19 J.

Wavelength: lambda = h c / E = (6.63 x 10^-34 x 3.0 x 10^8) / (8.5 x 10^-19). lambda = (1.989 x 10^-25) / (8.5 x 10^-19) = 2.34 x 10^-7 m.

Answer: 234 nm, as printed in the book.

20.4. Find the wavelength of the spectral line corresponding to the transition in hydrogen from n = 6 state to n = 3 state? (Book answer: 1094 nm)

Rydberg formula: 1 / lambda = R (1 / nf squared - 1 / ni squared), with nf = 3, ni = 6, R = 1.097 x 10^7 m^-1. 1 / lambda = (1.097 x 10^7) x (1 / 9 - 1 / 36) = (1.097 x 10^7) x (0.1111 - 0.0278).

1 / lambda = (1.097 x 10^7) x 0.0833 = 9.14 x 10^5 m^-1. lambda = 1 / (9.14 x 10^5) = 1.094 x 10^-6 m.

Answer: 1094 nm, as printed in the book.

20.5. Compute the shortest wavelength radiation in the Balmer series?

What value of n must be used? (Book answers: 364.5 nm, n = infinity) Balmer series: nf = 2. The shortest wavelength comes from the largest energy jump, ni = infinity.

1 / lambda = R (1 / 4 - 1 / infinity) = R / 4 = (1.097 x 10^7) / 4 = 2.74 x 10^6 m^-1. lambda = 1 / (2.74 x 10^6) = 3.645 x 10^-7 m.

Answers: 364.5 nm and n = infinity, as printed in the book.

20.6. Calculate the longest wavelength of radiation for the Paschen series.

(Book answer: 1875 nm) Paschen series: nf = 3. The longest wavelength comes from the smallest energy jump, ni = 4. 1 / lambda = R (1 / 9 - 1 / 16) = (1.097 x 10^7) x (0.1111 - 0.0625).

1 / lambda = (1.097 x 10^7) x 0.0486 = 5.33 x 10^5 m^-1. lambda = 1 / (5.33 x 10^5) = 1.875 x 10^-6 m.

Answer: 1875 nm, as printed in the book.

20.7. Electrons in an X-ray tube are accelerated through a potential difference of 3000 V. If these electrons were slowed down in a target, what will be the minimum wavelength of X-rays produced? (Book answer: 4.14 x 10^-10 m)

The most energetic X-ray photon takes the electron's full kinetic energy: E = e V = 3000 eV.

Minimum wavelength: lambda-min = h c / E = 1240 eV nm / 3000 eV = 0.413 nm. lambda-min = 4.13 x 10^-10 m, printed by the book as 4.14 x 10^-10 m.

Answer: 4.14 x 10^-10 m, as printed in the book.

20.8. The wavelength of K X-ray from copper is 1.377 x 10^-10 m. What is the energy difference between the two levels from which this transition results?

(Book answer: 9.03 keV) Energy difference: delta E = h c / lambda. lambda = 1.377 x 10^-10 m = 0.1377 nm. delta E = 1240 / 0.1377 = 9005 eV = 9.01 keV by this value of h c; the book prints 9.03 keV.

Answer: 9.03 keV, as printed in the book.

20.9. A tungsten target is struck by electrons that have been accelerated from rest through 40 kV potential difference. Find the shortest wavelength of the bremsstrahlung radiation emitted. (Book answer: 0.31 x 10^-10 m)

The shortest wavelength photon takes the electron's full energy: E = 40 keV. lambda-min = h c / E = 1240 eV nm / 40000 eV = 0.031 nm.

Answer: 0.31 x 10^-10 m, as printed in the book.

20.10. The orbital electron of a hydrogen atom moves with a speed of 5.456 x 10^5 m s^-1. (a) Find the value of the quantum number n associated with this electron. (b) Calculate the radius of this orbit. (c) Find the energy of the electron in this orbit. (Book answers: n = 4, rn = 0.846 nm; En = -0.85 eV)

Step 1: (a) Bohr speed: vn = (2.18 x 10^6) / n, so n = (2.18 x 10^6) / (5.456 x 10^5) = 4.0.

Step 2: (b) Radius: rn = n squared x r1 = 16 x (0.529 x 10^-10) = 8.46 x 10^-10 m = 0.846 nm.

Step 3: (c) Energy: En = -13.6 / n squared = -13.6 / 16 = -0.85 eV.

Answers: n = 4, rn = 0.846 nm and En = -0.85 eV, as printed in the book.

mcqs.why: In the ground state the kinetic energy is +13.6 eV and the potential energy is -2 x 13.6 = -27.2 eV. Total energy = 13.6 - 27.2 = -13.6 eV. (The orbit radius is 0.529 x 10^-10 m and the angular momentum is h / (2 pi) = 1.05 x 10^-34 kg m^2 s^-1.)

mcqs.why: With h c = 1240 eV nm, E = 1240 / lambda (in nm) = 1240 / 400 = 3.10 eV. (500 nm gives 2.49 eV as printed in the book, and 700 nm gives 1240 / 700 = 1.77 eV.)

mcqs.q: An electron jumps from a level Ei = -3.5 x 10^-19 J to Ef = -1.20 x 10^-18 J. The wavelength of the emitted light is:
The wavelength of the spectral line for the hydrogen transition from n = 6 to n = 3 is:

mcqs.why: For the Balmer series nf = 2, and the shortest wavelength comes from the largest energy jump, ni = infinity. 1 / lambda = R / 4 = (1.097 x 10^7) / 4 = 2.74 x 10^6 m^-1, so lambda = 1 / (2.74 x 10^6) = 3.645 x 10^-7 m = 364.5 nm.

mcqs.why: For the Paschen series nf = 3, and the longest wavelength comes from the smallest energy jump, ni = 4. 1 / lambda = R (1 / 9 - 1 / 16) = (1.097 x 10^7) x (0.1111 - 0.0625) = (1.097 x 10^7) x 0.0486 = 5.33 x 10^5 m^-1. lambda = 1 / (5.33 x 10^5) = 1.875 x 10^-6 m = 1875 nm.

mcqs.why: The most energetic photon takes the electron's full kinetic energy, E = e V = 3000 eV. lambda-min = h c / E = 1240 / 3000 nm = 0.413 nm = 4.13 x 10^-10 m by this value of h c, printed by the book as 4.14 x 10^-10 m.

mcqs.q: The K X-ray from copper has wavelength 1.377 x 10^-10 m. The energy difference between the two levels involved in the transition is:
mcqs.why: delta E = h c / lambda = 1240 / 0.1377 eV (with lambda = 0.1377 nm) = 9005 eV, about 9.01 keV with h c = 1240 eV nm; the book prints 9.03 keV, as recorded in the notes.

mcqs.q: Electrons accelerated from rest through 40 kV strike a tungsten target. The shortest wavelength of the bremsstrahlung radiation emitted is:
mcqs.why: The shortest wavelength photon takes the electron's full energy, E = 40 keV. lambda-min = h c / E = 1240 / 40000 nm = 0.031 nm = 0.31 x 10^-10 m.

mcqs.q: The orbital electron of a hydrogen atom moves with a speed of 5.456 x 10^5 m s^-1. The quantum number of its orbit is:

lessons.title: Review Questions
lessons.notes_html:
21.1. What are isotopes? What do they have in common and what are their differences?

Isotopes are nuclei of the same element that have the same atomic number Z but different mass numbers A.

In common: the same number of protons, the same number of electrons in the neutral atom, the same chemical properties, and the same place in the periodic table.

Differences: different numbers of neutrons, different masses, and often different nuclear stability: some isotopes are stable while others are radioactive.

21.2. Why are heavy nuclei unstable?

In a heavy nucleus there are many protons, and the repulsive Coulomb force between them grows rapidly with proton number.

The attractive strong nuclear force is short-ranged and saturates: each nucleon only attracts its near neighbours.

In heavy nuclei the repulsion eventually overpowers the attraction, so the nucleus cannot hold together permanently.

Heavy nuclei therefore decay by emitting radiation until they reach a more stable configuration.

21.3. If a nucleus has a half-life of 1 year, does this mean that it will be completely decayed after 2 years? Explain.

No, it does not mean that.

Half-life is a statistical law for a large sample, not a lifetime for one nucleus.

After 1 year, half of the sample remains; after 2 years, which is two half-lives, one quarter of the original sample still remains and three quarters have decayed.

The sample never becomes exactly zero: each half-life only halves what is left, and any single nucleus may survive many half-lives.

21.4. What fraction of a radioactive sample decays after two half-lives have elapsed?

After one half-life, 1/2 of the sample remains.

After two half-lives, 1/2 of that half remains, which is 1/4 of the original sample.

So the fraction that has decayed is 1 - 1/4 = 3/4 of the sample.

21.5. The radioactive element 226_88 Ra has a half-life of 1.6 x 10^3 years. Since the Earth is about 5 billion years old, how can you explain why we still can find this element in nature?

Radium-226 cannot be primordial: with a half-life of only 1600 years, any radium present when the Earth formed would have decayed away completely long ago.

It is still found because it is continuously being made.

Radium-226 is a daughter product in the uranium-238 decay series: uranium-238, with a half-life of 4.5 billion years, decays step by step through thorium and other elements to radium-226.

Fresh radium-226 is therefore constantly produced in uranium ores, which is why it is still present in nature.

21.6. Describe a brief account of interaction of various types of radiations with matter.

Alpha radiation consists of heavy, doubly charged particles: they interact very strongly with matter, ionize densely along a short track, and are stopped by a sheet of paper or a few centimetres of air.

Beta radiation consists of fast electrons: they are much lighter and singly charged, so they ionize less densely and travel further, being stopped by a few millimetres of aluminium.

Gamma radiation consists of uncharged photons: they do not ionize directly but knock electrons out of atoms by the photoelectric effect, Compton scattering and pair production, and those electrons then cause ionization.

Gamma rays are the most penetrating and need thick lead or concrete to stop them.

21.7. Explain how alpha and beta-particles may ionize an atom without directly hitting the electrons? What is the difference in the action of the two particles for producing ionization?

A charged particle need not strike an electron directly to ionize an atom.

Its electric field acts at a distance: as it passes near an atom, it pulls or pushes the atomic electrons with a Coulomb force.

If the energy transferred is enough, an electron is torn away and the atom is ionized.

The difference is in strength and density: an alpha particle carries charge +2e and moves slowly, so its field acts strongly and for longer, producing dense ionization along a short track.

A beta particle carries charge -e and moves much faster, so it produces sparser ionization spread over a longer track.

21.8. A particle which produces more ionization is less penetrating. Why?

Ionization costs the particle energy: every ion pair it creates takes energy from the particle.

A strongly ionizing particle loses its energy very quickly, so it is brought to rest after a short distance.

A weakly ionizing particle loses energy slowly and keeps most of it, so it travels much further into matter.

That is why alpha particles, which ionize most densely, penetrate least, while gamma rays, which ionize least directly, penetrate most.

21.9. What information is revealed by the length and shape of the tracks of an incident particle in Wilson cloud chamber?

The length of a track tells us the particle's range, and hence its energy: a longer track means a more energetic, more penetrating particle.

The thickness or density of droplets along the track tells us the ionizing power: a thick, dense track is an alpha particle, a thin, faint track is a beta particle.

The shape tells us about scattering: beta tracks are zigzag because the light electron is easily deflected, while alpha tracks are straight.

If a magnetic field is applied, the curvature of the track gives the sign of the charge and the momentum of the particle.

21.10. Why must a Geiger Muller tube for detecting alpha-particles have a very thin end window? Why does a Geiger Muller tube for detecting gamma-rays not need a window at all?

Alpha particles are stopped by the thinnest of materials, even a sheet of paper.

If the tube's end window were thick, the alpha particles would be absorbed in the window before reaching the gas inside, so the window must be extremely thin.

Gamma rays are so penetrating that they pass straight through the metal wall of the tube itself.

They are detected when they knock electrons out of the wall or gas inside the tube, so no window is needed at all.

21.11. Describe the principle of operation of a solid state detector of ionizing radiation in terms of generation and detection of charge carriers.

In a solid state detector, ionizing radiation enters a semiconductor crystal, such as silicon.

The radiation's energy creates electron-hole pairs in the crystal: each absorbed chunk of energy frees charge carriers.

An applied voltage sweeps the electrons to one electrode and the holes to the other.

The collected charge forms an electrical pulse whose size is proportional to the energy deposited by the radiation, so the detector both counts the particles and measures their energy.

21.12. What do we mean by the term critical mass?

Critical mass is the minimum mass of fissile material, such as uranium-235, needed to sustain a nuclear chain reaction.

In a smaller mass, too many neutrons escape through the surface, so on average fewer than one neutron from each fission causes another fission and the reaction dies out.

At the critical mass, on average at least one neutron per fission goes on to cause another fission, so the chain reaction sustains itself.

21.13. Discuss the advantages and disadvantages of nuclear power compared to the use of fossil fuel generated power.

Advantages of nuclear power: it produces no carbon dioxide or smoke during operation, so it does not add to global warming or air pollution.

A very small mass of fuel gives a very large amount of energy, so fuel transport and storage are easy.

Disadvantages: the waste stays radioactive for thousands of years and must be stored safely.

Accidents can release radioactivity, plants are expensive to build and to decommission, and the technology raises proliferation concerns.

Fossil fuel plants are cheaper and well established, but they burn huge quantities of fuel, emit carbon dioxide and pollutants, and depend on finite reserves.

21.14. What factors make a fusion reaction difficult to achieve?

Fusion is difficult because the nuclei to be fused both carry positive charge and repel each other strongly.

To overcome this Coulomb repulsion they must be heated to tens of millions of degrees, so that they move fast enough to collide and fuse.

At such temperatures the fuel is a plasma that must be confined without touching any wall, which is done with magnetic fields or by inertial confinement.

It is also hard to get more energy out of the reaction than is put in to heat and confine the plasma, and the intense neutrons produced damage the reactor materials.

21.15. Discuss the advantages and disadvantages of fission power from the point of safety, pollution and resources.

Safety: a fission reactor is designed with control rods, shielding and containment, but an accident or loss of cooling can release radioactive material, so strict safety systems are essential.

Pollution: fission power emits no carbon dioxide or smoke, but it produces long-lived radioactive waste that must be isolated for thousands of years, and uranium mining also causes environmental damage.

Resources: uranium is a finite resource, but because fission releases so much energy per kilogram, a small amount of fuel lasts a long time, and breeder reactors can extend the supply further.

21.16. What do you understand by "background radiation"? State two sources of this radiation.

Background radiation is the low level of ionizing radiation that is always present around us, from natural and man-made sources.

Two sources are: cosmic rays arriving from outer space, and natural radioactivity in rocks and soil, including radon gas that seeps into buildings from the ground.

21.17. If someone accidently swallows an alpha-source and a beta-source which would be the more dangerous to him? Explain why?

The alpha source would be more dangerous.

Outside the body, alpha particles are harmless because they are stopped by the skin.

Inside the body, the alpha emitter sits in direct contact with living tissue and deposits all of its energy in a tiny volume, causing intense local damage: alpha radiation has a high relative biological effectiveness.

A beta source inside the body is also dangerous, but beta particles are less ionizing and spread their energy over a larger volume, so the local damage is less severe.

21.18. Which radiation dose would deposit more energy to the body (a) 10 mGy to the hand, or (b) 1 mGy dose to the entire body.

Energy deposited = absorbed dose x mass of the tissue.

(a) Hand: mass about 0.5 kg, so energy = (10 x 10^-3) x 0.5 = 5 x 10^-3 J.

(b) Whole body: mass about 70 kg, so energy = (1 x 10^-3) x 70 = 70 x 10^-3 J.

So the whole-body dose deposits more total energy, about fourteen times as much, even though the hand dose is locally more intense.

Answer: (b), the 1 mGy dose to the entire body.

21.19. What is a radioactive tracer? Describe one application each in medicine, agriculture and industry.

A radioactive tracer is a small amount of a radioactive isotope used to follow a process: its radiation can be detected from outside, showing where the substance goes.

Medicine: iodine-131 is used to diagnose and treat thyroid disorders, because iodine concentrates in the thyroid gland.

Agriculture: phosphorus-32 is used to study how plants take up fertilizer from the soil.

Industry: tracers are injected into pipelines to locate leaks, or used to measure wear in engines by the radioactivity appearing in the lubricating oil.

21.20. How can radioactivity help in the treatment of cancer?

Cancer cells divide rapidly and repair radiation damage poorly, so they are more sensitive to radiation than most normal cells.

In radiotherapy, a carefully aimed beam of gamma rays, for example from cobalt-60, or a radioactive isotope placed inside the body, such as iodine-131 for thyroid cancer, damages the DNA of the cancer cells.

The damaged cells die or stop dividing, while the surrounding healthy tissue is spared as much as possible by precise targeting and by splitting the treatment into small doses.

mcqs.q: Isotopes are nuclei that have:
options: The same mass number A but different atomic numbers Z
The same atomic number Z but different mass numbers A, i.e. different numbers of neutrons
The same number of neutrons but different numbers of protons
Different chemical properties and different places in the periodic table
mcqs.why: Isotopes are nuclei of the same element: the same atomic number Z (same number of protons and, in the neutral atom, electrons), the same chemical properties and the same place in the periodic table. They differ in their numbers of neutrons and masses, and often in nuclear stability.

mcqs.q: Heavy nuclei are unstable because:
options: The strong nuclear force weakens with time
The repulsive Coulomb force between the many protons grows rapidly with proton number, while the attractive strong force is short-ranged and saturates
Heavy nuclei contain too many neutrons to hold any protons
mcqs.why: The strong nuclear force is short-ranged and saturates: each nucleon only attracts its near neighbours. The Coulomb repulsion between the many protons in a heavy nucleus keeps growing with proton number until it overpowers the attraction, so heavy nuclei decay by emitting radiation until they reach a more stable configuration.

mcqs.q: A radioactive sample has a half-life of 1 year. After 2 years:
options: One half of it will remain
One quarter of the original sample will remain
Three quarters of it will remain
mcqs.why: Half-life is a statistical law for a large sample. After 1 year half remains; after 2 years, two half-lives, half of that half remains, which is 1 / 4 of the original sample. The sample never becomes exactly zero, because each half-life only halves what is left.

mcqs.q: Radium-226, with a half-life of only 1.6 x 10^3 years, is still found in nature although the Earth is about 5 billion years old because:
options: It is continuously being made as a daughter product in the uranium-238 decay series
It was created recently by cosmic rays
It does not decay inside uranium ores
mcqs.why: Any primordial radium-226 would have decayed away long ago. It is still found because uranium-238, with a half-life of 4.5 billion years, decays step by step through thorium and other elements to radium-226, so fresh radium-226 is constantly produced in uranium ores.

mcqs.q: Which radiation is the most penetrating, and what stops it?
options: Alpha radiation, stopped by thick lead
Gamma radiation, stopped only by thick lead or concrete
Alpha radiation, stopped by a few millimetres of aluminium
mcqs.why: Alpha particles ionize densely and are stopped by a sheet of paper or a few centimetres of air. Beta particles (fast electrons) travel further and are stopped by a few millimetres of aluminium. Gamma rays, uncharged photons, are the most penetrating and need thick lead or concrete to stop them.

mcqs.q: A particle which produces more ionization is less penetrating because:
options: It moves more slowly through the material only
Every ion pair it creates takes energy from it, so a strongly ionizing particle loses its energy quickly and is stopped after a short distance
It is repelled by the atoms of the material
Its charge is neutralized at the surface
mcqs.why: Ionization costs the particle energy. A strongly ionizing particle loses its energy very quickly and is brought to rest after a short distance, while a weakly ionizing particle keeps most of its energy and travels much further. That is why alpha particles penetrate least and gamma rays penetrate most.

mcqs.q: A Geiger Muller tube for detecting alpha-particles must have a very thin end window because:
options: Alpha particles are stopped by even the thinnest of materials, so a thick window would absorb them before they reach the gas inside
The window must let light into the tube
Alpha particles are too large to pass a small window
Gamma rays must be kept out
mcqs.why: Alpha particles are stopped by the thinnest of materials, even a sheet of paper, so the end window must be extremely thin. A tube for gamma-rays needs no window at all, because gamma rays pass straight through the metal wall and are detected when they knock electrons out of the wall or gas inside.

mcqs.q: The critical mass of a fissile material is:
options: The largest mass that can be stored safely
The minimum mass needed to sustain a nuclear chain reaction
The mass converted into energy in one fission
The mass of the nucleus at which fission starts spontaneously
mcqs.why: Critical mass is the minimum mass of fissile material, such as uranium-235, needed to sustain a chain reaction. In a smaller mass too many neutrons escape through the surface and the reaction dies out; at the critical mass, on average at least one neutron per fission causes another fission.

mcqs.q: If someone accidentally swallows an alpha-source and a beta-source, which is the more dangerous, and why?
options: The beta-source, because beta particles are faster
The alpha-source, because inside the body it deposits all its energy in a tiny volume of living tissue, causing intense local damage
Both are equally harmless inside the body
The beta-source, because alpha particles are stopped by the skin
mcqs.why: Outside the body alpha particles are harmless because the skin stops them. Inside the body the alpha emitter sits in direct contact with living tissue and deposits all of its energy in a tiny volume: alpha radiation has a high relative biological effectiveness. Beta particles spread their energy over a larger volume, so the local damage is less severe.

mcqs.q: Which deposits more total energy in the body: (a) a dose of 10 mGy to the hand (mass about 0.5 kg), or (b) a dose of 1 mGy to the entire body (mass about 70 kg)?
options: (a) the hand dose, because 10 mGy is the larger dose
(b) the whole-body dose, about fourteen times as much energy
mcqs.why: Energy deposited = absorbed dose x mass. (a) Hand: (10 x 10^-3) x 0.5 = 5 x 10^-3 J. (b) Whole body: (1 x 10^-3) x 70 = 70 x 10^-3 J. So the whole-body dose deposits more total energy, about 70 / 5 = 14 times as much, even though the hand dose is locally more intense.

lessons.notes_html:
21.1. Find the mass defect and the binding energy for tritium, if the atomic mass of tritium is 3.016049 u. (Book answers: 0.00857 u, 7.97 MeV)

Tritium has 1 proton and 2 neutrons. From the book's table (book p. 222): proton mass = 1.007276 u, neutron mass = 1.008665 u.

Mass of the separate nucleons = 1.007276 + 2 x 1.008665 = 1.007276 + 2.017330 = 3.024606 u.

Mass defect = 3.024606 - 3.016049 = 0.008557 u, which the book rounds to 0.00857 u.

Binding energy = mass defect x 931.5 MeV/u = 0.00857 x 931.5 = 7.98 MeV, printed by the book as 7.97 MeV.

Answers: mass defect 0.00857 u and binding energy 7.97 MeV, as printed in the book.

21.2. The half-life of 91_38 Sr is 9.70 hours. Find its decay constant. (Book answer: 1.99 x 10^-5 s^-1)

Decay constant: lambda = 0.693 / T-half.

Half-life in seconds: 9.70 hours x 3600 = 34920 s. lambda = 0.693 / 34920 = 1.98 x 10^-5 s^-1, printed by the book as 1.99 x 10^-5 s^-1.

Answer: 1.99 x 10^-5 s^-1, as printed in the book.

21.3. The element 234_91 Pa is unstable and decays by beta-emission with a half-life 6.66 hours. State the nuclear reaction and the daughter nuclei. (Book answer: 234_92 U)

In beta-minus decay a neutron changes into a proton and an electron: the mass number stays the same and the atomic number increases by 1.

Reaction: 234_91 Pa -> 234_92 U + 0_-1 e.

The daughter nucleus is uranium-234: 234_92 U, as printed in the book.

21.4. Find the energy associated with the following reaction: (Mass of 1H = 1.00784 u) 14_7 N + 4_2 He -> 17_8 O + 1_1 H. What does negative sign indicate?

(Book answer: 1.12 MeV) From the book's table (book p. 222): nitrogen-14 = 14.0031 u, helium-4 = 4.0026 u, oxygen-17 = 16.9991 u; hydrogen-1 = 1.0078 u as given in the stem.

Mass of reactants = 14.0031 + 4.0026 = 18.0057 u.

Mass of products = 16.9991 + 1.0078 = 18.0069 u.

Mass change = 18.0057 - 18.0069 = -0.0012 u.

Energy: Q = (-0.0012) x 931.5 = -1.12 MeV.

The negative sign means the reaction is endoergic: the products are heavier than the reactants, so energy must be supplied, by the kinetic energy of the incoming alpha particle, for the reaction to happen.

Answer: -1.12 MeV (magnitude 1.12 MeV as printed in the book).

21.5. Determine the energy associated with the following reaction: (mass of 14C = 14.0077 u) 14_6 C -> 14_7 N + 0_-1 e. (Book answer: 3.77 MeV)

Parent: carbon-14 = 14.0077 u, as given in the stem.

Daughter: nitrogen-14 = 14.0031 u from the book's table (book p. 222); the book's working takes the mass difference as 14.0077 - 14.0031 - 0.00055 (one electron mass) = 0.00405 u.

Energy = 0.00405 x 931.5 = 3.77 MeV.

Answer: 3.77 MeV, as printed in the book.

Note: the stem's carbon-14 mass of 14.0077 u is the book's own figure; with the modern atomic mass of carbon-14 (14.0032 u) this decay energy would be only about 0.156 MeV.

21.6. If 233_92 U decays twice by alpha-emission, what is the resulting isotope? (Book answer printed as 225_88 Rn)

Each alpha emission reduces the mass number by 4 and the atomic number by 2.

After the first alpha: 233 - 4 = 229, 92 - 2 = 90, giving thorium-229.

After the second alpha: 229 - 4 = 225, 90 - 2 = 88.

The resulting isotope has mass number 225 and atomic number 88, which is radium-225: 225_88 Ra.

Note: the book prints the symbol as Rn, but atomic number 88 is radium (Ra); radon is atomic number 86. The numbers 225 and 88 are correct for radium-225.

21.7. Calculate the energy (in MeV) released in the following fusion reaction: 2_1 H + 3_1 H -> 4_2 He + 1_0 n. (Book answer: 17.6 MeV/event)

From the book's table (book p. 222): deuterium = 2.014102 u, tritium = 3.01605 u, helium-4 = 4.002603 u, neutron = 1.008665 u.

Mass of reactants = 2.014102 + 3.01605 = 5.030152 u.

Mass of products = 4.002603 + 1.008665 = 5.011268 u.

Mass defect = 5.030152 - 5.011268 = 0.018884 u.

Energy released = 0.018884 x 931.5 = 17.59 MeV.

Answer: 17.6 MeV per event, as printed in the book.

21.8. A sheet of lead 5.0 mm thick reduces the intensity of a beam of gamma-rays by a factor 0.4. Find half value thickness of lead sheet which will reduce the intensity to half of its initial value. (Book answer: 3.79 mm)

Intensity after thickness x: I = I0 e^(-mu x), so 0.4 = e^(-mu x 5.0).

Taking natural logs: ln(0.4) = -mu x 5.0, so mu = 0.9163 / 5.0 = 0.18326 mm^-1.

Half-value thickness: I / I0 = 1/2 = e^(-mu x-half), so x-half = ln 2 / mu = 0.693 / 0.18326 = 3.78 mm.

Answer: 3.79 mm, as printed in the book.

21.9. Radiation from a point source obeys the inverse square law. If the count rate at a distance of 1.0 m from Geiger counter is 360 counts per minute, what will be its count rate at 3.0 m from the source? (Book answer: 40 counts per min.)

Inverse square law: count rate is proportional to 1 / (distance squared).

At 3.0 m the distance is 3 times larger, so the count rate falls by a factor of 3 squared = 9.

Count rate = 360 / 9 = 40 counts per minute.

Answer: 40 counts per minute, as printed in the book.

21.10. A 75 kg person receives a whole body radiation dose of 24 m-rad, delivered by alpha-particles for which RBE factor is 12. Calculate (a) the absorbed energy in joules, and (b) the equivalent dose in rem. (Book answers: (a) 18 mJ (b) 0.29 rem)

Step 1: (a) Convert the absorbed dose: 24 m-rad = 0.024 rad. Since 1 rad = 0.01 Gy = 0.01 J/kg, the dose is 0.024 x 0.01 = 2.4 x 10^-4 J/kg.

Step 2: Absorbed energy = dose x mass = (2.4 x 10^-4) x 75 = 0.018 J = 18 mJ.

Step 3: (b) Equivalent dose = absorbed dose in rad x RBE = 0.024 x 12 = 0.288 rem.

Answers: (a) 18 mJ and (b) 0.29 rem, as printed in the book.
